Is Water Better Than Diet Soft Drinks For Weight Loss? A Two-Year Trial Put Them To The Test

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (449 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.
  • Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.
  • People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

Water and diet drinks went head to head in a two-year trial.

People who drink diet soft drinks can keep weight off for two years about as well as those who drink water.

Among those who completed the trial, average weight loss was 4.8 kg in the diet drink group and 3.7 kg in the water group (which was not a statistically significant difference).

Both groups took part in a weight management programme and remained lighter a year after regular support ended.

They also reported similar changes in hunger, despite the difference in how sweet their drinks tasted.

Almost 500 adults with overweight or obesity began the trial after being randomly assigned to drink water or commercially available diet drinks each day.

The study included regular diet drink consumers alongside those who rarely or never chose them.

Everyone began with 12 weeks of active weight loss, followed by 40 weeks of support to help them maintain their progress.

Sugar intake fell by similar amounts in both groups.

One theory is that people learn to expect energy when they taste something sweet.

If the expected calories fail to arrive, the theory goes, that mismatch might affect hunger and lead people to make up the difference by eating more later.

Comparing water with a diet soft drink allows researchers to ask whether sweet taste matters during weight management, since both drinks provide little or no energy.

By the end of the trial, hunger ratings had risen slightly in both groups, and the change was similar whether participants drank water or diet drinks.

Professor Joanne Harrold, the study’s first author, said:.

“These latest findings show that concerns about sweeteners disrupting appetite or causing weight gain are not supported when tested in a rigorous, long-term randomised trial.”.

When water or a diet drink replaces a sugary soft drink, the swap also cuts the calories in that serving.

A review of 17 randomised trials found small reductions in body weight when people replaced sugary drinks with low- or no-calorie sweetened alternatives, with results broadly similar to those for water (McGlynn et al., 2022).

The two-year trial adds a longer view of what happens when people keep the sweet taste in their drinks while working to maintain weight loss.

The study was published in the British Journal of Nutrition (Harrold et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean.

Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers

📅 09 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1227 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more.
  • Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs.
  • If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v5.4 update, you can now encode and compare texts, images, audio, and videos using the same familiar API. In this blogpost, I'll show you how to use these fresh multimodal capabilities for both embedding and reranking.

Multimodal embedding models map inputs from different modalities into a shared embedding space, while multimodal reranker models score the relevance of mixed-modality pairs. This opens up use cases like visual document retrieval, cross-modal search, and multimodal RAG pipelines.

If you want to train your own multimodal models, check out the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

Traditional embedding models convert text into fixed-size vectors. Multimodal embedding models extend this by mapping inputs from different modalities (text, images, audio, or video) into a shared embedding space. This means you can compare a text query against image documents (or vice versa) using the same similarity functions you're already familiar with.

Similarly, traditional reranker (Cross Encoder) models compute relevance scores between pairs of texts. Multimodal rerankers can score pairs where one or both elements are images, combined text-image documents, or other modalities.

For example, you can compare a text query against image documents, find video clips matching a description, or build RAG pipelines that work across modalities.

Multimodal models require some extra dependencies. Install the extras for the modalities you need (see Installation for more details):.

VLM-based models like Qwen3-VL-2B require a GPU with at least ~8 GB of VRAM. For the 8B variants, expect ~20 GB. If you don't have a local GPU, consider using a cloud GPU service or Google Colab. On CPU, these models will be extremely slow; text-only or CLIP models are better suited for CPU inference.

Loading a multimodal embedding model works exactly like loading a text-only model:.

In a recent development, some models might require a revision argument for now if the integration pull requests for the model is still pending. Once they're merged, you'll be able to load them without specifying a revision, like above.

The model automatically detects which modalities it supports, so there's nothing extra to configure. See Processor and Model kwargs if you want to control things like image resolution or model precision.

In a recent development, with a multimodal model loaded, model.encode() accepts images alongside text. Images can be provided as URLs, local file paths, or PIL Image objects (see Supported Input Types for all accepted formats):.

You can compute similarities between text embeddings and image embeddings, since the model maps both into the same space:.

Recent findings suggest that as expected, "A green car parked in front of a yellow building" is most similar to the car image (0.51), and "A bee on a pink flower" is most similar to the bee image (0.67). The hard negatives ("A red car driving on a highway", "A wasp on a wooden table") correctly receive lower scores.

You might notice that even the best matching scores (0.51, 0.67) aren't very close to 1.0. This is due to the modality gap: embeddings from different modalities tend to cluster in separate regions of the space. Cross-modal similarities are typically lower than within-modal ones (e.g., text-to-text), but the relative ordering is preserved, so retrieval still works well.

Industry observers note that for retrieval tasks, encode_query() and encode_document() are the recommended methods. Many retrieval models prepend different instruction prompts depending on whether the input is a query or a document, similar to how chat models might apply different system prompts depending on the goal. Model authors can specify their prompts in the model config, and encode_query() / encode_document() automatically load and apply the correct one:.

Industry observers note that under the hood, both are thin wrappers around encode(), they just handle prompt selection for you. Here's what cross-modal retrieval looks like:.

These methods accept the same input types as encode() (images, URLs, multimodal dicts, etc.) and pass through the same parameters. For models without specialized query/document prompts, they behave identically to encode().

Recent findings suggest that multimodal reranker (CrossEncoder) models score the relevance between pairs of inputs, where each element can be text, an image, audio, video, or a combination. They tend to outperform embedding models in terms of quality, but are slower since they process each pair individually. The currently available pretrained multimodal rerankers focus on text and image inputs, but the architecture supports any modality that the underlying model can handle.

The rank() method scores and ranks a list of documents against a query, supporting mixed modalities:.

Sources indicate that the reranker correctly identifies the car image (document 0) as the most relevant result, followed by the combined text+image document about a car in a European city (document 3). The bee image (document 1) scores lowest. Keep in mind that the modality gap can influence absolute scores: text-image pair scores may occupy a different range than text-text or image-image pair scores.

You can also check which modalities a reranker supports using modalities and supports(), just like with embedding models:.

You can also use predict() to get raw relevance scores for specific pairs of inputs:.

A common pattern is to use an embedding model for fast initial retrieval, then refine the top results with a reranker:.

According to recent reports, since the corpus embeddings are pre-computed, the initial retrieval is fast even over millions of documents. The reranker then provides more accurate scoring over the smaller candidate set.

Multimodal models accept a variety of input formats. Here's a summary of what you can pass to model.encode():.

You can check which modalities a model supports using the modalities property and supports() method:.

Recent findings suggest that the "message" modality indicates that the model accepts chat-style message inputs with interleaved content. In practice, you rarely need to use this directly. When you pass strings, URLs, or multimodal dicts, the model converts them to the appropriate message format internally. Sentence Transformers supports two message formats:.

The format is auto-detected from the model's chat template.

Since all inputs get converted into the same message format internally, you can mix input types in a single encode() call:.

If a model doesn't follow either format and you need full control, you can pass raw message dicts with role and content keys directly:.

This bypasses the automatic format conversion and passes the messages directly to the processor's apply_chat_template().

Industry observers note that you may want to control image resolution bounds or model precision. Use processor_kwargs and model_kwargs when loading the model:.

See the SentenceTransformer API Reference documentation for more details on these kwargs.

Recent findings suggest that in Sentence Transformers v5.4, tokenizer_kwargs has been renamed to processor_kwargs to reflect that multimodal models use processors rather than just tokenizers. The old name is still accepted but deprecated.

Here are the multimodal models supported in v5.4, also available in the v5.4 integrations collection:.

The older CLIP models continue to be supported:.

These simple CLIP models still work well on lower-resource hardware.

To learn how to finetune these multimodal models on your own data, see the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models with Sentence Transformers.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When I research a topic through long-form podcasts or university lectures (say, sleep architecture, creatine for cognition, or semiconductor supply chains), I keep hitting two annoying walls:.
  • Over the past few weeks I built PastNoise to scratch that exact itch.
  • Filtering sponsor reads before picking clips (not after) Early builds looked fine until a flagship topic pulled two Hostinger and Tonal ad reads from top podcasts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When I research a topic through long-form podcasts or university lectures (say, sleep architecture, creatine for cognition, or semiconductor supply chains), I keep hitting two annoying walls:.

Over the past few weeks I built PastNoise to scratch that exact itch. Instead of generating another text summary, it searches across 206M+ timestamped spoken subtitle lines and stitches 5 to 6 non-duplicate primary speakers into a single continuous screening room, paired with side-by-side Wikipedia, PubMed, Crossref, and OpenAlex citations.

Sources indicate that 1. Filtering sponsor reads before picking clips (not after) Early builds looked fine until a flagship topic pulled two Hostinger and Tonal ad reads from top podcasts. Moving a strict sponsor/outro detector ahead of act selection and hydrating 16 candidate windows first (then backfilling clean distinct channels) dropped sponsor contamination to zero across all 58 indexed screenings.

2. Rendering full bilingual transcripts in SSR DOM with #act-X-t-Y citation anchors Single-page tabs that unmount transcript DOM hide 95% of spoken text from search engines and make it impossible to quote a speaker accurately. Keeping every chapter's timestamped transcript inside lightweight accordions with click-to-copy citation links lets readers jump straight to the exact second and verify the primary quote.

In a recent development, 3. Preserving original subtitle sequence IDs (origSeq) when splitting long cues Auto-captions often pack 220+ characters into one cue. Splitting cues down to readable 96-character lines broke pre-translated subtitle lookups whenever the original sequence index passed 100. Keeping an explicit origSeq field alongside sequential display IDs solved alignment cleanly for English, Simplified Chinese, and Traditional Chinese (via OpenCC at zero extra LLM cost).

If you prefer local notes or want clean benchmark data for citation-grounded RAG experiments, I exported the entire 58-topic curated archive under CC BY 4.0:.

Tech Report: Granite 4.1 LLMs: How They’re Built

📅 29 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1720 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.
  • TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens.
  • Building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An in-depth technical walkthrough of data engineering, pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning behind the Granite 4.1 LLMs.

TL;DR — Granite 4.1 is a family of dense, decoder‑only LLMs (3B, 8B, and 30B) trained on ~15T tokens using a multi‑stage pre‑training pipeline, including long‑context extension of up to 512K tokens. The models are further refined with supervised fine‑tuning on ~4.1M high‑quality curated samples and reinforcement learning via on‑policy GRPO with DAPO loss (Yu et al., 2025). Notably, the 8B instruct model matches or surpasses the previous Granite 4.0‑H‑Small (32B‑A9B MoE) despite using a simpler dense architecture with fewer parameters. All Granite 4.1 models are released under the Apache 2.0 license.

Building high‑quality small language models goes beyond simply scaling compute—it requires rigorous data curation throughout training. For Granite 4.1, we prioritized data quality over quantity, progressively refining the data mixture across five pre‑training stages. We further curated supervised fine‑tuning data using an LLM‑as‑Judge framework and applied a multi‑stage reinforcement learning pipeline to systematically strengthen performance in math, coding, instruction following, and general chat.

Industry observers note that granite 4.1 models use a decoder-only dense transformer architecture. The core design choices include Grouped Query Attention (GQA), Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), SwiGLU activations, RMSNorm, and shared input/output embeddings.

All three model sizes share the same training pipeline and data strategy, differing only in architecture dimensions.

According to recent reports, granite 4.1 is trained from scratch on approximately 15 trillion tokens using a five‑phase training strategy. Phases 1–2 focus on foundational pre‑training, phases 3–4 perform mid‑training with progressively higher‑quality data annealing, and phase 5 introduces long‑context training, extending the context window to 512K tokens. Each phase employs a distinct data mixture and learning‑rate schedule, gradually shifting from broad web‑scale data to more curated, domain‑specific content.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2: The five-phase pre-training pipeline. Phases 1–2 are pre-training, Phases 3–4 are mid-training (high-quality data annealing), and Phase 5 is long context training (LCE).

The first phase establishes broad language understanding using a general mixture of training data with a power learning rate schedule and warmup.

Phase 2 sharply increases the proportion of code and mathematical data, pivoting toward stronger reasoning capabilities while still maintaining general language coverage.

Phase 3 transitions into mid-training with a more balanced, high-quality mixture and an exponential decay learning rate schedule. This is where we start blending in chain-of-thought and synthetic instruction data.

The fourth phase continues mid-training with a linear learning rate decay to zero, focusing the model on the highest-quality data available.

Figure 3: How the data mix evolves across the pre-training phases. Notice the progressive shift from web-heavy (Phase 1) to quality-heavy with instruction and reasoning data (Phases 3–4).

The fifth and final phase also part of of mid-training extends the context window from 4K to 512K through a staged long-context extension process:.

The LCE phase uses an exponential learning rate schedule starting at 1e-4 and decaying to 0. To ensure the model natively handles long sequences without degrading short-context performance, we do a model merge after each LCE stage. RULER benchmark of base models:.

Industry observers note that supervised fine‑tuning (SFT) is what turns the base model into a reliable instruction‑following assistant, making data quality critically important—since even a small number of incorrect or hallucinated samples can instill undesirable behaviors. To address this, we apply a rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework alongside rule‑based filtering to curate high-quality samples. Together, the pipeline automatically assess each sample against structural, semantic, and behavioral criteria, fixing issues when possible and filtering out samples that fail to meet our quality standards.

Figure 4: The SFT data quality pipeline. Raw conversation data passes through an LLM-as-Judge with a multi-dimensional rubric, producing accept/borderline/reject verdicts. Hard-reject defects (hallucination, false premise, incorrect computation) trigger automatic rejection regardless of score.

Sources indicate that our rigorous LLM‑as‑Judge framework evaluates only assistant responses, treating system prompts, user inputs, retrieved documents, and tool outputs strictly as contextual information. This ensures that the judge assesses what the model claims, rather than what it was asked to do. In RAG settings, responses that are not grounded in the retrieved context are flagged as hallucinations, while tool‑use outputs are validated against the set of allowed tools and their parameter schemas.

It has been revealed that we employ specialized judge prompts tailored to different SFT data types, including multi‑turn dialogue, RAG‑augmented responses, tool‑calling interactions, and multilingual conversations. Each response is scored across six weighted dimensions—instruction following, correctness, completeness, conciseness, naturalness, and calibration (with optional critical‑thinking checks). Samples are accepted, flagged as borderline, or rejected based on deterministic score thresholds, with hard‑reject rules overriding scores for severe defects such as hallucinations, false premises, or incorrect computations.

Recent findings suggest that to complement semantic evaluation, we apply a deterministic rule‑based pipeline that enforces structural integrity through text normalization, truncation and length filtering, schema validation, and leakage detection. A final global deduplication step ensures dataset‑wide uniqueness. All filtering and correction actions are fully auditable.

Sources indicate that after passing through the LLM-as-Judge, rule-based filtering, and global deduplication pipeline, we fine-tune base models on these approximately 4.1 million high-quality samples. The following details apply to all three model variants:.

Industry observers note that after SFT, we apply a multi-stage reinforcement learning pipeline to further improve the model's capabilities across specific domains. Rather than a single RL pass, we run multiple targeted RL stages, each optimizing for different capabilities.

We use On-policy GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) (Shao et al., 2024) with DAPO (Decoupled Clip and Dynamic sAmpling Policy Optimization) loss (Yu et al., 2025) which provides more stable training signals compared to standard GRPO. However, due to computationally intensive nature of dynamic sampling, we switch it off during our training runs.

According to recent reports, figure 10 depicts our Reinforcement Learning pipeline for training Granite 4.1 models. Through extensive experimentation with a variety of reinforcement learning recipes, we found that this sequence of steps minimizes catastrophic forgetting while simultaneously maximizing performance across multiple domains.

Figure 10: The Granite 4.1 reinforcement learning pipeline consisting of four sequential stages: Multi-domain RL, RLHF, Identity and Knowledge-calibration RL, and Math RL.

Recent findings suggest that in this stage, the model is trained jointly on a unified mixture of data drawn from multiple domains. Every gradient revision therefore reflects the full diversity of tasks, which prevents catastrophic forgetting, boosts overall benchmark performance, and minimizes regressions on any individual task.

The different domains covered in this stage include:.

During this stage, we trained the models on 45,504 unique prompts (averaged across all Granite 4.1 models) and found that a learning rate of 5e‑7 with a KL‑loss coefficient ($\beta$) of 0.05 performed best for multi‑domain reinforcement learning.

Recent findings suggest that to further improve the model's helpfulness and chat ability, we train our model on generic-chat prompts using a multilingual scalar reward model. With this stage, we observed an average improvement of ~18.9 points (averaged across the three Granite 4.1 models) in Alpaca-Eval compared to the SFT checkpoints.

Sources indicate that to mitigate policy drift from its previously learned knowledge, we use a conservative learning rate of 3e-7 and higher KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09 in this stage. We use an average of 17,920 unique prompts in this RLHF stage.

In this stage, we train the model for a few steps (~40 training steps) on identity and knowledge calibration prompts. We observed that this small training stage significantly improves the model's self-identification capabilities.

Similar to the RLHF stage, we used a learning rate of 3e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.09, and we use 1728 unique prompts in this stage.

It has been revealed that during our RL training, we found that the RLHF stage causes a drop in math benchmark scores (e.g., in GSM8K, DeepMind-Math). The Math RL stage enables the model to recover from this drop and surpasses the original SFT performance on math benchmarks: ~3.8 points on average for GSM8K, and ~23.48 points on average for DeepMind-Math. We use an average of 13,504 unique prompts in this stage and similar to the multi-domain RL stage, we used a learning rate of 5e-7 and KL-loss coeff $\beta$ of 0.05.

Supported languages: English, German, Spanish, French, Japanese, Portuguese, Arabic, Czech, Italian, Korean, Dutch, and Chinese.

Granite 4.1 delivers competitive instruction‑following and tool‑calling capabilities without relying on long chains of thought. By avoiding extended reasoning traces, it provides predictable latency, stable token usage, and lower operational cost. This makes Granite 4.1 a production‑ready, open‑source choice for enterprise workloads where efficiency, reliability, and cost control are critical.

A striking result: the Granite 4.1-8B dense model consistently matches or outperforms the previous-generation Granite 4.0-H-Small, a 32B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 9B active parameters.

Figure 13: Granite 4.1-8B (dark blue) vs. Granite 4.0-H-Small 32B-A9B (light blue) across benchmarks. The 8B dense model matches or exceeds the larger MoE model on IFEval, AlpacaEval, MMLU-Pro, BBH, GSM8K, DeepMind-Math, Evalplus, ArenaHard, BFCL V3 and MBPP(+).

Industry observers note that figure 14: Comparison across the Granite 4.1 family — 30B, 8B, and 3B models. Scores scale predictably with model size, with the 30B model leading across all benchmarks.

Industry observers note that we also released fp8 quantized variants of the Granite 4.1 models, optimized for inference with vLLM. The precision is reduced from 16‑bit to 8‑bit, resulting in approximately a 50% reduction in both disk footprint and GPU memory usage. Quantization is applied only to the weights and activations of linear operators within the transformer blocks using LLM Compressor, while all other layers are preserved at their original precision.

We trained the Granite 4.1 Language Models on an NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 cluster hosted on CoreWeave:.

This infrastructure provides the scalable, high-bandwidth interconnect needed for efficient distributed training at the token volumes required (15T+ tokens across pre-training alone).

Granite 4.1 models are available under the Apache 2.0 license. Here's how to get started with the 30B instruct model wiht tool calling example:.

In a recent development, granite 4.1 marks a significant step forward for high‑quality, open‑source language models. By prioritizing data quality and rigor at every stage—from pre‑training curation to supervised fine‑tuning and multi‑stage reinforcement learning—we deliver a substantially improved post‑training pipeline. The result is stronger instruction following, tool use, and conversational performance, showing that carefully trained dense 8B models can rival much larger MoE architectures. We’re excited to see how the community adopts and builds on these models.

#57672. The Tasks of Mathematicians and Software Engineers Are Converging in the Age of AI

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (168 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

The Tasks of Mathematicians and Software Engineers Are Converging in the Age of AI

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (168 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that with the emergence of AI, the work of software engineers and mathematicians is beginning to converge in a surprising way: both increasingly write prompts to generate code. The difference lies mainly in what kind of code they want. A software engineer might ask, “Write a Rust function to sort a list of numbers,” or “Write a Python script to analyze this dataset.” A mathematician might ask, “Write a Lean proof that the sum of two even numbers is even.” In each case, the human expresses an idea in natural language, and AI translates it into a formal language: Rust or Python for software, Lean for mathematics. The generated code may still need correction, but the underlying workflow is becoming remarkably similar. Software engineers prompt AI to build programs; mathematicians prompt AI to build formal proofs. This convergence suggests a future in which the ability to formulate precise ideas becomes increasingly important, whether one is developing software or proving theorems.

Breaking: The Positive Personality Trait Linked To Having A Crush Outside Your Relationship

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (514 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?
  • What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?
  • Both positive and dark personality traits are linked to becoming infatuated with someone outside a committed relationship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

Both positive and dark personality traits are linked to becoming infatuated with someone outside a committed relationship.

The clearest link among the dark traits is with psychopathy, which includes impulsivity and a lack of empathy.

Yet a more positive trait, the tendency to see value in other people and admire their qualities, is also linked to stronger infatuation once other differences are taken into account.

The researchers suggest that impulsivity may make a upcoming attraction more rewarding, while an appreciation of other people may make it easier to form an emotional connection with them.

People who are more open to casual sex or less satisfied with their relationship also report stronger feelings for someone else.

The study involved just over 300 adults in Romania who were in committed relationships.

They completed questionnaires about their personality, their attitudes and experiences around casual sex, and how satisfied they were with their relationship.

The researchers also asked about the thoughts, feelings and desires people had towards someone other than their partner.

Psychologists call this extradyadic infatuation, a preoccupation that can involve repeatedly thinking about someone and feeling unable to tell your partner how strongly you feel.

People who scored higher on humanism, the tendency to value and admire others, generally reported less infatuation outside their relationship.

Of all the factors the researchers examined, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation after the others were taken into account.

The researchers suggest that people high in humanism may be more receptive to forming a close connection with someone new.

Faith in humanity, which reflects a belief in other people’s goodwill, highlighted a different pattern and remained linked to less infatuation.

People who expect others to be dependable may also see their existing relationship as more secure and feel less drawn to alternatives, the researchers suggest.

Machiavellianism, a tendency to approach relationships strategically and manipulate others for personal gain, also indicated a reversal.

It was linked to stronger infatuation when examined on its own and to weaker infatuation once the other factors were considered.

The researchers suggest that someone who takes a calculating approach to relationships may be wary of an outside attachment that demands sustained emotional investment.

Psychopathic traits, by comparison, were linked to stronger infatuation in both analyses.

When the researchers compared all the factors together, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation.

Dissatisfaction with an existing relationship may also make an alternative partner seem more appealing, although the survey leaves open whether dissatisfaction precedes the infatuation or follows it.

The study was published in the journal Psychological Reports (Huţanu & Holman, 2026).

#57667. OAuth mix-up defense needs the RFC 9207 issuer response check

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (722 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

OAuth mix-up defense needs the RFC 9207 issuer response check

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (722 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that an OAuth client that supports more than one authorization server has a routing problem that ordinary state validation does not solve.
  • The check is small, but its placement matters.
  • RFC 9207 indicates an authorization server that supports the specification must include iss in authorization responses.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that an OAuth client that supports more than one authorization server has a routing problem that ordinary state validation does not solve. A malicious authorization server can return an authorization response that the client mistakes for one from a trusted server. RFC 9207 addresses this class of mix-up attacks by adding an iss parameter to the authorization response. The value identifies the authorization server that created the response, including error responses. The client then compares it with the issuer value it trusts for that authorization transaction.

The check is small, but its placement matters. It belongs before the client exchanges an authorization code. The callback handler should already know which issuer it selected for the transaction from server-side state or another protected correlation record. It should not infer the expected issuer from the callback parameters, because the attacker controls those parameters along with the response.

RFC 9207 indicates an authorization server that supports the specification must include iss in authorization responses. Clients interacting with an authorization server that publishes OAuth metadata must compare the response value with the metadata issuer. The RFC defines the value as the issuer identifier from the server metadata, not a display name, hostname fragment, or tenant label invented by the client. Clients should use an exact comparison and maintain one canonical representation of each issuer.

RFC 9700 places this mechanism among the recommended defenses against authorization server mix-up. The larger defense still depends on transaction binding. The client needs to remember the selected authorization server, redirect URI, PKCE verifier, state value, and other transaction-specific data in a protected location. The iss parameter makes the server's identity explicit, but it does not repair a transaction that was already confused before the callback arrived.

According to recent reports, the authorization server metadata should advertise authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported when the server supports RFC 9207. A client integration should reject a response whose iss is missing when that protection is required by policy, or whose value does not exactly match the issuer selected for the transaction.

Error responses need the same treatment. A login failure, consent denial, or temporary server error can still move a client into a branch that logs, retries, or exchanges a code. If a client only checks iss on successful callbacks, a mixed-up error path can still produce the wrong behavior.

In a recent development, the expected issuer should come from a configured trust entry, not from the query string. For a multi-tenant service, the entry should identify the exact tenant or realm if those values produce separate issuer identifiers. A trailing slash, case difference, or different URL form can make string comparison fail. Choose one canonical issuer value in configuration and compare that value consistently.

In a recent development, OIDC clients also need to validate the ID token issuer. An iss parameter in the authorization response and an iss claim in a token answer related but separate questions. The response parameter identifies the server that created the response. The token issuer claim is evaluated as part of token validation. One check does not replace the other.

Recent findings suggest that start with metadata discovery. Record which authorization servers advertise RFC 9207 support and which clients can enforce it. Add a negative test that sends a response with a missing or wrong iss and confirms that no token exchange occurs. Add a successful test for each configured issuer, including issuers that use different tenant identifiers.

Legacy servers that do not support the parameter need an explicit migration decision. A client can keep a narrowly scoped compatibility path while the server is upgraded, but that path should be visible in configuration and retired. Silently accepting a missing issuer prevents the organization from knowing which integrations are protected.

In a recent development, log the expected issuer, the received issuer when present, the authorization server configuration entry, and the transaction identifier. Do not log authorization codes, PKCE verifiers, access tokens, or other credentials. A mismatch should produce a security event and stop the flow, not a retry against another issuer.

The iss response parameter is useful because it closes a routing ambiguity at the point where the response enters the client. It remains one part of a chain that includes exact redirect URI matching, PKCE, state validation, token audience checks, and a clear trust configuration.

#57666. Stop Calling Every Chatbot an Agent: The Goal Plan Act Loop That Actually Earns the Name

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1010 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dev ↗ Open Full Page

Stop Calling Every Chatbot an Agent: The Goal Plan Act Loop That Actually Earns the Name

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, short answer: a chatbot takes a prompt and returns an answer.
  • It has been revealed that according to SmashingApps.com, generative AI creates content — text, images, audio — from prompts.
  • According to recent reports, generative AI runs on Request → Response.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, short answer: a chatbot takes a prompt and returns an answer. An agent takes a goal, breaks it into steps, calls tools, checks its own results, and keeps going until the goal is done — or stops. That loop is Goal → Plan → Act → Evaluate → Iterate, and if your system does not have it, it is not an agent, no matter what the marketing page indicates.

It has been revealed that according to SmashingApps.com, generative AI creates content — text, images, audio — from prompts. Agentic AI goes further: it sets goals, plans multi-step actions, uses tools, and takes semi-autonomous actions to achieve outcomes. The difference is not the model. It is the loop around the model.

According to recent reports, generative AI runs on Request → Response. You ask, it answers, the conversation ends. That is enough for drafting, summarising, and brainstorming, and it is where most "AI features" still live.

Agentic AI runs on Goal → Strategy → Act → Evaluate → Iterate. You set a goal. A planner breaks it into tasks. An executor calls tools — search, APIs, a database. An evaluator checks the results and decides what to do next. The loop repeats until the goal is reached or the system stops. That is the whole definition, and it is testable: if you remove the loop, does the system still do the job? If yes, it was never an agent.

According to recent reports, an agent is built by combining generative capabilities with orchestration logic, memory, and tool access. In practice that means three parts: an LLM for planning and reasoning, a tool registry it can call, and an execution controller that runs the loop and keeps a log.

Anthropic draws an important architectural distinction in its guide to Building effective AI agents: workflows are systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths, while agents are systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage, maintaining control over how they accomplish tasks. Both are agentic systems. Only the second one is an agent in the strict sense.

It has been revealed that and here is the part most teams skip: Anthropic found, working with dozens of teams, that the most successful implementations were not using complex frameworks or specialised libraries. They were building with simple, composable patterns. Start with the simplest solution possible, and only increase complexity when needed. For many applications, a single LLM call with retrieval and in-context examples is enough — no agent required.

It has been revealed that first, a research agent. Give it a goal: find three recent blog posts on remote-work productivity with their key findings. It searches the web for competitor pricing and posts, compiles a spreadsheet, emails the results to you, and schedules a follow-up meeting. No human touched the middle steps. The loop did the work.

In a recent development, second, an operations automation. It monitors servers, triages alerts, attempts a safe restart, and notifies the on-call engineer if the problem persists. Again, the value is not the model writing a status message. It is the system acting, checking whether the restart worked, and escalating when it did not.

If your "agent" cannot show you that loop — goal, initiative, tool calls, evaluation, iteration — it is a chatbot with a workflow diagram.

Agentic systems trade latency and cost for better task performance, so the tradeoff has to make sense. Ask three questions before you build one.

Sources indicate that first, is the task actually multi-step and unpredictable? If the steps are fixed and known in advance, a workflow with predefined code paths is cheaper, faster, and easier to debug. Use a workflow.

According to recent reports, second, can a single LLM call with retrieval do it? If yes, do that. Adding an agent loop to a one-shot task adds failure modes for no benefit.

According to recent reports, third, what happens when it goes wrong? An agent that can send emails, run code, or touch production data needs guardrails before it needs features. If you cannot answer that question, you are not ready to give it tools.

If you do give a system agency — let it act — these are the non-negotiables, in order.

Industry observers note that give it the least privilege possible: only the tools and permissions it absolutely needs. Nothing else.

Keep a human in the loop: require explicit review for high-impact actions — payments, deletions, legal messages, anything you cannot undo.

Log everything: plans, tool calls, and decisions, with an explainable transcript you can audit later.

Add rate limiting and kill switches, so a runaway loop stops instead of burning your budget or spamming your people.

Validate and sandbox: test agents in isolated environments before production, validate and sanitise any data they use when calling external systems, and start with manual review for the first 100 runs before switching to more autonomy.

There is one more pattern worth knowing, because it is where the token bill explodes. In a multi-agent system, a lead agent looks the work and subagents explore different parts of it in parallel, each with its own context window, before condensing the findings back. Anthropic's multi-agent research system works this way, and it outperformed a single-agent setup by a wide margin on its internal research eval — but multi-agent systems used about 15 times more tokens than a standard chat interaction. That is a fair trade for a hard research problem. It is a terrible trade for a task a single call could have done.

Generative AI answers. Agentic AI acts, checks, and iterates. The test is simple: show me the loop. Goal, plan, tools, evaluation, iteration — with logging and a human gate on anything irreversible. Build the simplest thing that passes that test, and stop calling the rest agents.

For the full comparison, including the design patterns, the safety checklist, and how to choose between the two, see the complete guide to agentic AI vs generative AI on SmashingApps.com.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I built Bazaar Ledger, a shop bookkeeping app for Android with a Windows companion, and I want to share what offline-first did to the design.

According to recent reports, the rule. Every bill, payment and stock movement is written to the phone first. The network is optional, so there is no loading spinner between a customer and a receipt.

The ledger underneath. Billing screens are friendly, but every sale, payment, purchase and expense posts to double-entry accounts. That is why the 100+ reports agree with each other: they are different views of one ledger.

A server that cannot read. If a shop turns on the optional cloud, the books are sealed on the phone before upload, with keys the server never receives. The cost is real: the server cannot search, repair or analyse a shop's data, so every feature that needs reading has to be opt-in and done on the device.

Industry observers note that posted bills are never edited in place. A correction is a cancelled bill plus a fresh corrected one, both kept, behind a PIN. It is more work to build and far easier to audit.

The AI assistant is optional and narrow. Simple commands are parsed on the phone. When the phone is unsure, the assistant (Anthropic's Claude, through our server) gets only what that one request needs, never the whole book. You review and save by default.

Sources indicate that the app is free for one whole shop. I would like feedback from other Flutter developers on two things: testing sync conflicts when two counters sell the last unit offline, and how you handle thousands of ledger rows on low-end phones.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
  • Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.

These drugs block the action of acetylcholine, a chemical messenger in the brain and body, and are used to treat depression, overactive bladder and symptoms of Parkinson’s disease.

For example, amitriptyline is an antidepressant formerly sold as Tryptizol in the UK and Elavil in the US.

Oxybutynin, used to treat overactive bladder, also has anticholinergic effects and comes in patches known as Kentera in the UK and Oxytrol in the US.

In a study of more than 217,000 people, each additional anticholinergic medicine prescribed at the start was associated with a 15 per cent higher rate of dementia diagnosis in the UK group and about a 6 per cent higher rate in the US group.

Acetylcholine helps the brain pay attention, learn and form memories.

In the bladder, blocking certain acetylcholine signals can help control involuntary contractions.

Blocking those signals in the brain can make it harder to concentrate and may cause confusion.

Other tricyclic antidepressants with anticholinergic effects include clomipramine, known by the brand name Anafranil in both countries, and nortriptyline, known as Allegron in the UK and Pamelor in the US.

Paroxetine, an SSRI antidepressant with anticholinergic effects, has been sold as Seroxat in the UK and Paxil in the US.

Some antipsychotics also have these effects, including olanzapine, known as Zyprexa in both countries and used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

The medicines have different uses, which makes their shared effect easy to overlook when someone takes several prescriptions for unrelated conditions.

Using a list of 88 medicines, the researchers counted how many each person had been prescribed at the start of the study.

They then looked at dementia diagnoses over a median of about 16 years in the UK Biobank and nine years in the US All of Us Research Program.

About a quarter of participants in the British group and just over a fifth of those in the American group had been prescribed at least one medicine on the list.

The increases were relative, and fewer than two in 100 participants in each group were diagnosed with dementia during follow-up.

The percentages describe how the rate of dementia diagnosis varied with the number of medicines prescribed and give no risk estimate for any individual drug.

A prescription can reveal something about a person’s health as well as what medicine they have been given.

Depression and Parkinson’s disease, for example, can lead to anticholinergic prescribing and are themselves associated with dementia risk.

The researchers could account for some differences in health between participants, but the reasons for prescribing and the severity of those conditions could still explain part of the association.

A count taken at the start also gives only a snapshot, since people may change medicines or stop taking them over the years.

For someone taking several prescriptions, a prescriber or pharmacist can review the full list and weigh the benefits and risks of each medicine in context.

The study was published in the journal Age and Ageing (Asiimwe et al., 2025).

The $30,000 average wedding figure you see everywhere is misleading. That number is skewed upward by luxury weddings in expensive metros like New York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. The national median — the number where half of weddings cost more and half cost less — sits closer to $10,000 to $15,000. That distinction matters because it means a beautiful, memorable wedding is absolutely possible without spending five figures you do not have.

Recent findings suggest that the FI perspective adds another layer: every dollar spent on a wedding is a dollar that cannot compound for decades. A $30,000 wedding invested for 30 years at a 7% average annual return grows to roughly $228,000. That does not mean you should elope in a courthouse (unless you want to), but it does mean you should spend intentionally on the categories that matter most to you and cut ruthlessly everywhere else.

The biggest takeaway from this table: venue and catering are 60-70% of the total. If you can reduce those two categories, you change the entire math.

Recent findings suggest that not all wedding spending creates equal memories. Research consistently shows that couples remember three things most vividly years later: the ceremony itself, the food and drinks, and the photographs. Almost nobody remembers the chair covers, the napkin folds, or the custom monogram on the cocktail napkins.

That insight creates a clear FI-aligned strategy: splurge on what creates lasting memories (photographer, food, music) and minimize everything else.

The golden rule of wedding budgeting: if you cannot remember whether a detail was present at the last three weddings you attended, your guests will not notice either. Cut it without guilt.

The biggest financial mistake couples make is not setting a firm budget before visiting any vendors. Venues and vendors are skilled at upselling, and without a hard number in mind, costs spiral promptly. Start with a number you can pay in cash — wedding debt is one of the worst ways to begin a marriage and a direct threat to your FI timeline.

If your budget is $15,000 and your wedding is 15 months away, that is $1,000 per month. Treat it like any other savings goal on your FI path — automate, do not touch, and watch it grow.

For couples on the FI path, consider this reframe: every dollar you shave from the wedding budget is a dollar that starts compounding immediately. Cutting $5,000 from a $20,000 wedding and investing that savings at 7% for 25 years creates roughly $27,000 in future wealth. You can have a wonderful wedding and build wealth simultaneously — but only if you plan intentionally from the start.

This is not an argument against celebrating — it is an argument for spending intentionally on what matters to you and cutting everything else. The link was more pronounced among girls and teenagers.

Children and teenagers who report frequent or severe headaches tend to have lower vitamin D levels.

The link was modest overall but stronger among girls and among teenagers.

Body mass index, or BMI, accounted for about a fifth of the association in the researchers’ statistical model.

One possibility is that vitamin D and body weight are both related to inflammation, which can affect how sensitive the nervous system is to pain.

Another is that young people who get frequent headaches spend less time outdoors, where sunlight helps the skin produce vitamin D.

The researchers analysed data collected between 2001 and 2004 as part of a US national health and nutrition survey.

The final analysis included just over 5,000 children and teenagers aged six to 19 who had the measurements needed for the study.

The researchers compared blood vitamin D levels with questionnaire reports of frequent or severe headaches, including migraines, in the previous year.

Almost a quarter had experienced headaches that met the survey’s description.

Because the survey grouped several types of headache together, it could not show whether the link was stronger for migraine.

The researchers suggest that inflammation could make pain-sensing nerves more sensitive, making mild discomfort feel more intense.

Low vitamin D and higher BMI can both occur alongside increased inflammation, which could help explain why the three measures were related.

For example, a teenager who regularly misses outdoor activities because of headaches may get less sun.

Diet is another possibility, since vitamin D can come from foods as well as sunlight.

The survey gave researchers a snapshot, so it could not show whether lower vitamin D preceded the headaches or followed them.

The study was published in the journal Medicine (Zhang et al., 2026).

#57654. Tech Report: Newark Museum of Art restores ownership of David Drake jug to artists’ descendants

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (635 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Newark Museum of Art restores ownership of David Drake jug to artists’ descendants

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (635 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This past summer, the Newark Museum of Art in Upcoming Jersey initiated a dialogue with the family of David Drake (around 1801-74), the enslaved potter from South Carolina, regarding a large brown ceramic jug in its collection, dated 1852.
  • The arrangement comes just over a year after the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston reached an historic agreement with Drake’s family to return two major stoneware vessels, one of which the museum purchased back.
  • Recent findings suggest that “What happened this July was really special,” indicates George Fatheree, an adviser to the Drake family.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This past summer, the Newark Museum of Art in Upcoming Jersey initiated a dialogue with the family of David Drake (around 1801-74), the enslaved potter from South Carolina, regarding a large brown ceramic jug in its collection, dated 1852. Just a few months later—lightning speed in museum time—The Art Newspaper has learned that the institution has reached an agreement with Drake’s heirs to restore ownership of the work and purchase it back for its permanent collection.

The arrangement comes just over a year after the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston reached an historic agreement with Drake’s family to return two major stoneware vessels, one of which the museum purchased back. Momentum built from there and return agreements were reached with institutions including the Telfair Museums in Savannah and the Georgia Museum of Art in Athens, Georgia, the Virginia Museum of Fine Arts, and others.

Recent findings suggest that “What happened this July was really special,” indicates George Fatheree, an adviser to the Drake family. A letter the Newark Museum sent to the artist’s descendants and shared with The Art Newspaper states: “We acquired a jug by your ancestor in 2022 to help us more powerfully teach the history of enslavement and enslaved labour, as part of the 2023 reimagining and reinstallation of our American art galleries, Seeing America: 18th and 19th Century.” Noting the MFA Boston partnership, the museum extended the opportunity to meet and “identify ways we might collaborate”.

According to Lisa Funderburke, the Newark Museum’s director and chief executive, it was the museum’s senior director of registration and collections management, Amber Germano, who first approached her over the summer and asked if she would be willing to sign a letter.

“It’s not uncommon for curators to visit my office with a stack of papers of things that are either for consideration or ongoing engagement on articles of repatriation,” Funderburke says. “Always my first question is: ‘Can you articulate to me what we’re doing here and what the impulse behind that is?’”.

According to Yaba Baker, one of Drake’s fourth great-grandsons, Funderburke credited her staff with the initial action. “Lisa understood immediately what needed to be done,” Baker claims. “One thing my family all agreed on: Dave is such a powerful figure in art history and Black history that to take the pots out of public view would be a disservice.”.

Industry observers note that things moved quickly after that, with additional family meetings and Funderburke’s conversations with board members and other leaders at the museum. “I felt like this would be a strong north star for our board about where we are and where we want to be, and position ourselves as a museum into the future,” the director notes.

After the museum commissioned several appraisals of the ceramic vessel, a value of around $135,000 was decided on. Numerous Drake pots have sold for five- and six-figure prices; the current record at auction for one of his works is the $1.65m paid for his 25-Gallon Poem Jar (1858), achieved at Crocker Farm Auctions in Maryland in 2021.

“Our approach is this should not be a zero-sum game,” Fatheree claims, describing the outcome in Newark as a “win-win”.

According to recent reports, baker concurs, stressing the enduring lessons of Drake’s legacy. “He was a slave. He was considered three fifths of a person by the US constitution,” Baker says, adding that anti-literacy laws in South Carolina at the time forbade teaching enslaved people to write.

“For our family, it’s telling the story of someone who was considered by a lot of people to be nothing, but he conducted himself with such excellence,” Baker indicates, before quoting a famous inscription Drake wrote on another of his vessels that begins, “I wonder where is all my relation”, and concludes: “Friendship to all.”.

Latest Update: New York auction houses hope single-owner collections will fuel $2.4bn week of sales

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1301 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that upcoming York’s major auction houses are heading into the November marquee sales next week with a sustained sense of confidence, as the global art market continues to show signs of recovery and a set of significant single-owner collections comes on the market.
  • The confident estimates for this month’s top lots—and strong results for Upcoming York’s May sales—resonate with an ArtTactic report released earlier this year, which found the top auction houses made strong recoveries during the first half of 2026.
  • Sources indicate that that consignment strategy will be on full display at Upcoming York’s blockbuster auctions next week.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that upcoming York’s major auction houses are heading into the November marquee sales next week with a sustained sense of confidence, as the global art market continues to show signs of recovery and a set of significant single-owner collections comes on the market. Sotheby's, Christie's, Phillips and Bonhams expect to bring in at least $2.04bn collectively from their auctions in the Big Apple this month, with sales potentially exceeding $2.4bn, slightly above last year’s estimates for the period.

The confident estimates for this month’s top lots—and strong results for Upcoming York’s May sales—resonate with an ArtTactic report released earlier this year, which found the top auction houses made strong recoveries during the first half of 2026. Global auction sales were up 70% year on year at Christie's, Sotheby's and Phillips in the first six months of the year, thanks in part to the enduring appeal of single-owner collections and major estates.

Sources indicate that that consignment strategy will be on full display at Upcoming York’s blockbuster auctions next week. Single-owner collections allow the houses to rebrand regular seasonal auctions as can’t-miss, once-in-a-lifetime events, and craft marketing campaigns around not just the works on sale but also the legacies of the collectors.

Van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890) Courtesy Sotheby's.

Sotheby’s boasts the highest collective estimate of the auction houses, projecting more than $1.1bn, which would be a house record for a marquee sale season. Around 40% of that total is attributed to the Blaquier-Arrieta collection, a fully guaranteed group of 12 Impressionist, Post-Impressionist and Fauvist paintings expected to sell for around $450m, making it the highest-value single-owner collection on offer this season across the city.

In a recent development, the collection was assembled by the Argentine sugar magnate Carlos Pedro Blaquier and his wife, María Elena “Nelly” Arrieta de Blaquier. Blaquier faced charges relating to the kidnapping of suspected left-wing activists during Argentina's 1976-83 military dictatorship. He denied the allegations and died in 2023 without standing trial. The 12 paintings have been consigned by the couple’s five children; the auction on 18 November will immediately be followed by Sotheby’s multiple-owner evening sale of Modern art.

“The market is very much moved by these collections,” states Allegra Bettini, Sotheby’s head of Modern evening auction. “Collectors today like to understand a narrative and see where works are coming from to understand the taste of how they all hung together.”.

When the works in the Blaquier-Arrieta hoard were acquired, mostly in the 1960s and 70s in Europe, collectors could still purchase museum-quality works by Modern masters from commercial art galleries. That is no longer the case, Sotheby’s specialists say, even with a seven-figure budget. The Blaquier-Arrieta family rarely, if ever, loaned works for public display. Until Sotheby’s put them on view in its galleries at the Breuer Building on the Upper East Side, few of the 12 consigned works had been on public exhibit or offered on the market in decades.

The trove’s headline lot is Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (1890), one of the final works the artist painted in Auvers-sur-Oise in the months before his death. It carries a staggering estimate of around $180m and, because it has been guaranteed, is sure to exceed the current auction record for a Van Gogh of $117m (including fees), set by Orchard with Cypresses (1888) at the Paul Allen sale at Christie’s New York in 2022.

“It’s hard to not want to just touch and feel these brushstrokes because it is so alive,” Bettini states, gesturing to the leaves of the trees in the painting. “There's an intensity to it that really brings us into this landscape with the artist.”.

Paul Cezanne’s Arlequin (1888–90) Courtesy Sotheby's.

Another possible recordbreaker is Arlequin (1888–90) by Paul Cezanne, which is estimated to sell in the region of $120m. The late harlequin painting is the only example from Cezanne’s series still in private hands, according to Sotheby’s. The current auction record for a Cezanne work, also set during the Paul Allen sales at Christie’s, is $137.79m.

In a recent development, other standout works from the Blaquier-Arrieta collection include paintings by Camille Pissarro, Claude Monet and Pierre-Auguste Renoir. Sotheby’s will also offer works from the collections of oil tycoon Armand Hammer, Seattle property developer Richard Hedreen and his wife Elizabeth Hedreen, and cable television pioneer Theodore Baum and his wife Ruth Baum.

According to recent reports, in Midtown at Christie’s, the leading lot of the season is Wassily Kandinsky's Betonte Ecken (1922-23), from the artist’s Bauhaus period. Once part of the Guggenheim collection, it was purchased by its current owners—reportedly the billionaire, art-dealing Nahmad family—at Sotheby’s in 1986. It is estimated to sell for between $60m and $80m during the 20th-century evening sale on 17 November.

With the same estimate and on offer during the same sale, Gustav Klimt’s landscape Litzlbergkeller (1915-16) was once part of the collection gathered by Serge Sabarsky, the late art dealer who co-founded the Neue Galerie in New York (the beloved Austrian restaurant on the museum’s ground floor is named for him). Leading the 21st century evening sale is an untitled 1983 work by Jean-Michel Basquiat that references a drawing on paper by Leonardo da Vinci and is estimated to sell for between $30m and $50m.

Wassily Kandinsky’s Das bunte Leben (1907) Courtesy Christie’s.

Christie’s is also offering a wide variety of works from the holdings of well-known collectors, among them the music executive Clive Davis, the billionaire businessman William Koch, and more works belonging to the late Museum of Modern Art trustee Agnes Gund that will benefit her foundation. Also on offer is a group of seven works including Old Master, Modernist and post-war artists understood to have been consigned by Jeff Koons. Altogether, the auction house expects to take in between $823m and $1.1bn during its November sales in Latest York.

Recent findings suggest that despite recent stock market volatility following the “blue tsunami” during the US midterm elections earlier this month and concerns over a Democrat-controlled Congress’s regulation of artificial intelligence and datacentre development—heightened by recent revelations about chipmaker Nvidia’s president Jensen Huang being embroiled in a spy scandal—stocks show early signs of stabilising. Christie’s specialists are similarly optimistic ahead of the November auctions.

It has been revealed that while fluctuations in the stock markets can influence the art market over the longer term, the immediate impact on high-end auctions tends to be limited. Particularly for evening auctions, where lots are estimated to sell for seven-, eight- and nine-figure sums, potential buyers are often wealthy enough to be insulated from the day-to-day fluctuations of the stock market.

Sources indicate that “The art’s quality is going to supersede any day in the market. People aren’t day-trading Picassos,” states Kat Widing, Christie’s senior vice president, senior specialist in post-war and contemporary art, and head of the 21st-century evening sale.

Industry observers note that collectors are “looking at these works over months, and they’re thinking through these major purchases”, she adds. “These would be additions to major collections that are quite significant. With those two things in mind, I’m still very optimistic.”.

Constantin Brâncuși bronzes up for auction this month at Bonhams Courtesy Bonhams.

Phillips expects to bring in between $80.4m and 128.7m in Upcoming York this month, with its auctions led by Amedeo Modigliani’s limestone sculpture Tête (1911-12), estimated to sell for between $28m and $35m after having been in the same private collection for more than 50 years.

Bonhams estimates it will sell at least $40m worth of art in November in New York, with most of that total coming from a collection of five fresh-to-market Constantin Brâncuși bronzes that were held in the same private collection for decades after being acquired from the artist’s estate. Collectively, they are expected to fetch $25m.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

People lacking this vitamin probably also have high blood pressure and heart disease.

A deficiency in vitamin D is linked to a doubling in the risk of heart disease.

After exposure to sunlight, vitamin D is produced in the skin and converted to calcifediol in the liver and then converted to calcitriol in the kidney.

Calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D) is an active form of vitamin D affecting the immune system, bone growth, the production of adrenaline, noradrenaline, dopamine, and serotonin.

A study suggests that calcitriol can also influence cardiovascular health through its effects on other systems, including the immune system.

In this research, participants with low levels of vitamin D appeared to have higher blood pressure and heart disease risk compared to people with adequate blood levels of vitamin D.

The results indicated that people with the lowest levels of vitamin D were twice as likely to suffer from cardiovascular disease than those within the normal range.

Cardiovascular disease (CVD) is a major cause of death and disability, killing 7.9 million people around the world each year.

Over a billion people globally have low levels of vitamin D.

The best test to determine vitamin D status is measuring the serum concentrations of 5-hydroxyvitamin D (25(OH)D).

To investigate the association between serum 25(OH)D levels and CVD risk, the research team analysed UK Biobank data on over half-a-million participants.

They found that the risk of high blood pressure and heart disease steeply decreased where the serum 25(OH)D level was around 50 nmol/L.

Over 55 percent of participants had serum levels of < 50 nmol/L and 13 percent were deficient with levels below 25 nmol/L.

The number of people with serum levels less than 50 nmol/L has been estimated to be 37 percent for Canada, 24 percent for USA, and 23 percent for Australia.

Professor Elina Hyppönen, the study’s leader, stated:.

“Severe deficiency is relatively rare, but in settings where this does occur it is very important to be proactive and avoid negative effects on the heart.

For example, deficiency can be a problem for people living in residential care who may have limited exposure to sun.”.

Vitamin D can be found in some foods but this amount is not enough.

“We can also get vitamin D from food, including oily fish, eggs and fortified foods and drinks.

This mentioned, food is unfortunately a relatively poor source of vitamin D, and even an otherwise healthy diet does not typically contain enough.

If we don’t get any vitamin D through the sun, this is one of the rare nutrients for which we sometimes need to take a daily supplement to keep up with the requirements.

Understanding the connection between low levels of vitamin D and CVD is especially key, given the global prevalence of this deadly condition.

Our results are exciting as they suggest that if we can raise levels of vitamin D within norms, we should also affect rates of CVD.

In our study population, by increasing vitamin D-deficient individuals to levels of at least 50 nmol/L, we estimate that 4.4 percent of all CVD cases could have been prevented.”.

The study was published in European Heart Journal  (Zhou et al., 2021).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

One type of question can indirectly reveal a lot about a person’s personality.

Asking someone what they think about other people reveals much about their own personality.

The reason is that people tend to see more of their own qualities in others.

The generous person sees others as generous and the selfish person sees others as selfish.

Dr Dustin Wood, the study’s first author, remarked:.

“A huge suite of negative personality traits are associated with viewing others negatively.

The simple tendency to see people negatively indicates a greater likelihood of depression and various personality disorders.”.

The conclusions come from a series of three studies.

In one people were asked to judge the positive and negative characteristics of three other people.

The more positively they judged those people, the more happy, enthusiastic, capable and emotionally stable they turned out to be themselves.

People who judged others more positively also turned out to be more satisfied with their own lives.

Set against this, those who judged others more negatively had higher levels of narcissism and antisocial behaviour.

The researchers even returned to the same people a year later and found the results were the same.

This suggests that what people’s ratings of others say about themselves remains stable over time.

Personality disorders are often diagnosed at least partly by how people view others, the authors write:.

“…although narcissists may perceive others as being uninteresting or worthless, this may not reflect how they see themselves.

Similarly, individuals displaying behaviors typical of paranoid personality disorder may believe that others are malevolent and untrustworthy, even though they may not see themselves that way.

Machiavellianism is usually measured in part by asking individuals the extent to which they perceive a lack of sincerity, integrity, or selflessness in others’ actions, and narcissistic behavior is thought to be prompted in part by a belief that other people are inferior, uninteresting, and unworthy of attention.”.

The study was published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology (Wood et al., 2010).

Under the curator Ekow Eshun, the upcoming 13th edition of the Site Santa Fe International Biennial, There Are Other Worlds (11 June 2027-10 January 2028), will aim to reflect how artists open up new ways of understanding the world, potentially inspiring connection and kinship amid the complexity of our times. The exhibition’s citywide programming will span more than six venues, bringing together more than 40 artists from over 15 countries. The biennial is due to include new commissions by the US artists Cauleen Smith, Sanford Biggers and Edgar Arceneaux, the New Mexico-based Diné artist Raven Chacon and the Canadian artist Lotus Kang.

Industry observers note that founded in 1995, Site Santa Fe is one of the US’s key contemporary art events, showcasing international artists while building on New Mexico’s history and social fabric. Eshun—who chairs the Fourth Plinth in London’s Trafalgar Square and is the curator of the touring British Art Show 10: A Chorus of Strangers (touring the UK until June 2028)—is drawing inspiration from the region.

Industry observers note that “New Mexico has a layered history, including colonial settlements, but also in the 20th century it had artistic communities that found something here that allowed them to think with expansiveness,” Eshun tells The Art Newspaper. “It is the site of settlement, world-making and self-discovery.”.

Site Santa Fe, Marlene Nathan Meyerson Auditorium entrance Photo: Shayla Blatchford, 2024; courtesy Site Santa Fe.

Sources indicate that beyond New Mexico, Eshun’s vision explores how artists challenge, interpret and shape reality. “We live in a time of divisiveness, uncertainty, inequality and environmental crisis,” he says. “I am inspired by how, in contrast, artists hold complexity and contradictions, inviting us to look beyond binary positions and consider other ways of seeing the world.” These might include imaginative, psychological, emotional and sensory worlds.

The sprawling exhibition is structured into three sections, the curator explains, conceived as “interlocking territories”. The first, “Worlds Beyond”, explores sensory and psychological perception, drawing on the legacy of the Transcendental Painting Group that was active in Fresh Mexico in the 1930s and 40s. “I am interested in how artists look beyond the physical world and can be inspired to think metaphysically, psychologically and emotionally,” Eshun indicates. He cites the participating Danish Icelandic artist Olafur Eliasson, who thinks with scientific precision while creating works that have both sensorial and emotional impacts.

The exhibition’s second section,“Worlds in Common”, draws on Upcoming Mexico’s history of utopian settlements to explore “how artworks may enable us to move beyond hierarchies of power or status and conjure connection or kinship, finding imaginative ways in which we can relate to each other”, Eshun states. He cites the work of Chacon as an example, which uncovers histories of displacement in the Americas, but also turns to connection and memory as routes to reimagining assertions of place.

Tavares Strachan's Black Madonna (Louise Little and Malcolm X) (2022) Courtesy the artist and Perrotin. Photo: Claire Dorn; courtesy Site Santa Fe.

It has been revealed that the exhibition’s third section,“Worlds Alive”, will focus on interactions with nature, considering “the planet as a living territory where all the creatures may have a say in how we live collectively”, Eshun states. He is particularly interested in artists who imagine a relationship with the planet beyond extractivism and grounded in connection across organisms. The participating Colombian artist Delcy Morelos, for instance, reflects on the earth as a physical and ethical territory and a space for aesthetic adventure.

The line-up of participating artists, spanning generations and geographies, reflects the curator’s intention to create a locally rooted biennial with an international scope. “The biennial exists in conversation, not isolation,” Eshun says, adding that community programming will be key. Nearly half the artists are from the US, including Arthur Jafa and Nan Goldin, while five, such as the Indigenous artists Rose B. Simpson and Cannupa Hanska Luger, are based in Newly introduced Mexico. The exhibition will also include a large contingent of international participants, such as Louise Giovanelli (UK), John Akomfrah (Ghana/UK), Sandra Vásquez de la Horra (Chile), Shilpa Gupta (India) and Tavares Strachan (Bahamas), among others.

While touching on pressing problems, Eshun hopes the biennial will also carry a sense of possibility, empathy and even optimism. Artists, he states, “offer no answers but may open fresh ways to see, imagine and engage with the present”.
