📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.
  • People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.
  • People with higher levels of vitamin D tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

People with higher levels of a common vitamin tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

People with higher levels of vitamin D tend to carry less fat around their internal organs.

This deeper layer of belly fat, known as visceral fat, surrounds organs such as the liver and intestines.

It matters because people with more visceral fat tend to have greater difficulty using insulin to control their blood sugar.

The link with vitamin D became weaker when the researchers took body mass index into account, suggesting that overall body size could explain part of the difference.

One possibility is that vitamin D is spread through a larger volume of tissue in people with more body fat, leaving a lower concentration in the blood.

The researchers reviewed records from nearly 1,300 adults with type 2 diabetes who attended a hospital in Quzhou, China, during a two-and-a-half-year period.

Each person had a blood test for vitamin D and a measurement to estimate their visceral fat.

The researchers divided patients into four groups according to their vitamin D levels and compared the estimated area of visceral fat in each group.

The clearest difference was between the groups with the highest and lowest vitamin D levels, with the middle groups showing a less consistent pattern.

After accounting for BMI and other differences between patients, the researchers estimated that the group with the highest vitamin D levels had about 10 square centimetres less visceral fat area than the group with the lowest levels.

Earlier research using genetic data suggested that a higher BMI can contribute to lower vitamin D levels, with weaker evidence for an effect in the other direction (Vimaleswaran et al., 2013).

As well as being distributed through a larger volume of tissue, some vitamin D may be stored in fat tissue, which could affect how much circulates in the blood.

Everyday habits could also help explain why the two measures vary together.

Someone who exercises outdoors may get more sunlight and carry less belly fat, two differences that could help explain the link.

The hospital records did not capture how much sunlight participants got, how active they were or whether they took vitamin D supplements.

Since vitamin D and belly fat were assessed at the same visit, it remains unclear which changed first or whether both were influenced by other factors.

The study was published in the Journal of International Medical Research (Zhu et al., 2026).

Artist captures the saga of Luigi Mangione in tweets

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that “The compression of anger and joy that I was seeing people write that day was astonishing,” Kahn tells The Art Newspaper; she immediately felt compelled to capture the torrent of reactions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the morning of 4 December 2024, the Los Angeles-based artist Stanya Kahn opened X (formerly Twitter) to get her daily news digest, when she, like many Americans, was inundated with a mass chorus of tweets—ranging from celebratory snark to unbridled vitriol—about the assassination of United HealthCare’s chief executive Brian Thompson.

Sources indicate that “The compression of anger and joy that I was seeing people write that day was astonishing,” Kahn tells The Art Newspaper; she immediately felt compelled to capture the torrent of reactions. “At first I was bookmarking them, and then [screenshotting] them, and fairly promptly my thought was to gather these up because the algorithm might start shutting them down.”.

According to recent reports, fairly promptly, the Trump administration announced that any celebration of the killing could be criminalised. But with an ever-growing archive and a long-held practice as a time-based media artist, Kahn decided to create a film that chronologically presented the public’s rapidly unfolding response to this now-infamous event.

Flyer for Deny, Defend, Depose (2026) Courtesy of Stanya Kahn.

Industry observers note that titled Deny Defend Depose (2026)—a play on the words scrawled on three shell casings from bullets fired in the shooting, and the strategy invoked by major healthcare providers to reduce payouts and increase profits—Kahn’s film is now screening across the country at artist-run-spaces, cinemas and galleries. The New York non-profit space Participant Inc will screen it on 13 November, with more showings to come.

Originally, Kahn planned to release the film in the lead-up to 9 September, when the state trial of Luigi Mangione was due to take place in Latest York. Now that Mangione’s 14 August guilty plea—an attempt to avoid double jeopardy—has postponed the state hearing until 10 December, with a federal hearing to follow on 18 December, Kahn plans to continue updating the film with more responses from the public as the saga continues.

According to recent reports, when it all began, she had considered turning the project into a coffee-table book, which would afford a funny inversion of X’s quippy, short-form format. But switching to a film, her primary medium, afforded an opportunity for in-person film screenings, which enabled the originally solitary experience of watching the commentary unfold online to be transformed into a collective viewing experience.

Stanya Kahn, Deny, Defend, Depose (2026, still), 30:28 min Courtesy of the artist.

Set to a dramatic soundtrack of acid and jungle, the 30-minute film takes viewers on an emotional rollercoaster. Watching the tweets unfold in sequence together, the audience collectively holds its breadth as anticipation builds to the moment the suspect is revealed as Mangione, laughs as tweets comment on his attractiveness or the Monopoly money found in his backpack, and sighs at the devastating state of healthcare in the United States when statistics regarding industry salaries and investment patterns, or personal anecdotes about life-threatening denials, are shared.

Sources indicate that just like Kahn was glued to X that morning in late 2024, viewers of her film are often transfixed as they relive their reactions to the still-unfolding story at top speed.“The poignancy of such a broad spectrum of the American public responding in kind to what was basically a public political assassination felt like a rupture, especially in party-based politics,” Kahn indicates. “It cut across the entire political spectrum and the common ground that suddenly emerged in this flashpoint seemed like a newly introduced beacon for potential mass movement, because it was a unity that emerged spontaneously and instantaneously, it wasn’t something that got hammered out in time.”.

Recent findings suggest that the outpouring of affection for Mangione has been staggering, Kahn says. “Without blinking,” she adds, “people were in full-throat applause of [an alleged] murderer.”.

Stanya Kahn, Deny, Defend, Depose (2026, still), 30:28 min Courtesy of the artist.

Attention from the media and public has remained steady since the early days of the manhunt, Mangione’s arrest and the trial, with comparisons to Robin Hood, lookalike contests and wanted posters for other healthcare firm executives. While the extent of the public’s celebration of Thompson’s killing took many by surprise, Kahn sees this reaction as evidence of just “how deep the pain and anger and frustration is in this country about the evilness of the healthcare system and its inaccessibility”. (Per capita spending on healthcare in the US is double the average of other wealthy countries, and has been increasing faster than inflation for decades.).

In a recent development, thompson’s killing and its aftermath are hardly a black-and-white tale of righteous moral vengeance. Though some originally attempted to paint Mangione as disaffected and radicalised, his Ivy League education and privileged upbringing told a different story. And the responses to the event “weren’t just coming from more radical spaces”, Kahn notes. While capturing their reactions in real time and reviewing the posters’ profiles, she found, “it was literally just ‘every man’—people with five followers and five million. It was regular people because they were pissed.”.

Older Brains Lose Synchronization Between Movement and Body Temperature

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A chronobiology study in mice reveals that while the brain’s 24-hour circadian rhythms persist into old age, shorter multi-hour “ultradian” rhythms in physical activity and core body temperature significantly weaken.
  • It has been revealed that throughout every 24-hour day, mammalian physiology follows an intricate temporal choreography.
  • Layered atop this overarching 24-hour cycle are faster, multi-hour biological oscillations known as ultradian rhythms, which pulse every few hours to coordinate bursts of activity, metabolic demand, and thermoregulation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A chronobiology study in mice reveals that while the brain’s 24-hour circadian rhythms persist into old age, shorter multi-hour “ultradian” rhythms in physical activity and core body temperature significantly weaken. Simultaneously, aging decouples movement from internal temperature regulation and triggers neuroinflammatory gene shifts, glial remodeling, and neuronal loss inside the brain’s master circadian clock, the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN).

It has been revealed that throughout every 24-hour day, mammalian physiology follows an intricate temporal choreography. Governed by the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), a tiny cluster of neurons in the hypothalamus that acts as the brain’s master biological clock, core body temperature, hormone release, and physical activity rise and fall in predictable ~24-hour circadian rhythms.

Layered atop this overarching 24-hour cycle are faster, multi-hour biological oscillations known as ultradian rhythms, which pulse every few hours to coordinate bursts of activity, metabolic demand, and thermoregulation.

While age-related sleep fragmentation and impaired temperature regulation are well-documented clinical hallmarks of aging, precisely how ultradian rhythms evolve across the lifespan, and how they relate to cellular changes inside the SCN, has remained poorly understood.

Now, a comprehensive chronobiology investigation examining mice across the adult lifespan (from 3 to 21 months of age) reveals that while the 24-hour circadian framework remains detectable in old age, the faster 2- to 6-hour ultradian rhythms deteriorate, accompanied by a breakdown in coordination between physical activity and internal body temperature.

To separate externally driven daily routines from internally generated biological timing, the researchers continuously recorded locomotor activity and core body temperature in mice across multiple age brackets under both standard 12-hour light/12-hour dark cycles and constant darkness, an experimental condition that removes environmental light cues to expose the brain’s intrinsic pacemaker.

The physiological telemetry revealed a striking divergence between macro- and micro-rhythms:.

To explore the neural underpinnings of these physiological shifts, the investigators analyzed cellular architecture and gene expression profiles directly inside the SCN of young and aged mice.

Even though core circadian clock genes continued cycling, the cellular microenvironment of the aging SCN demonstrated pronounced signs of biological wear:.

By demonstrating that shorter ultradian rhythms and temperature-activity coupling falter even when overall 24-hour circadian rhythmicity persists, the findings offer a fresh lens through which to view age-related sleep disturbances and vulnerability to heat or cold stress.

Further experimental work will determine whether targeting neuroinflammation or supporting glial-neuronal communication inside the SCN can restore ultradian stability, potentially paving the way for interventions that alleviate sleep fragmentation and thermoregulatory decline in older adults.

What is the difference between circadian rhythms and ultradian rhythms?

Industry observers note that circadian rhythms are biological cycles that repeat roughly every 24 hours, such as the daily sleep-wake cycle. Ultradian rhythms are shorter biological cycles that repeat multiple times within a single day, typically every 2 to 6 hours, regulating smaller bursts of physical activity, alertness, and core body temperature fluctuations.

How does aging affect these biological rhythms?

Researchers found that while older mice kept their basic 24-hour rhythms and core clock gene cycles, their shorter 2- to 6-hour ultradian rhythms weakened significantly. Furthermore, physical movement and internal body temperature became disconnected, no longer rising and falling together as closely as in younger animals.

What changes happen inside the brain’s master clock during aging?

Inside the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), the brain’s master clock, aging was linked to increased activity of immune-related genes, changes in supportive glial cells, and a reduction in neuron density, which may impair how the brain coordinates fine-tuned daily bodily rhythms.

Funding: This study was supported by JSPS KAKENHI (grant numbers JP21K19287, JP21H05036, JP23H04941, and JP22K21351); AMED (grant number JP21zf0127005); JST CREST (grant number JPMJCR24T4); JST SPRING (grant number JPMJSP2124) and the World Premier International Research Center Initiative (WPI).

Aging remodels the suprachiasmatic nucleus and weakens ultradian rhythms and activity–temperature coupling.

Aging alters daily physiology, but how these changes relate to remodeling of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) remains incompletely understood.

Here, we examined time-resolved SCN transcriptomic profiles alongside longitudinal recordings of core body temperature and locomotor activity, using separate cohorts for the molecular and physiological analyses.

Aging was associated with extensive SCN transcriptomic remodeling, including enrichment of innate immune, interferon-related, complement-associated, and glial programs, while selected canonical clock genes retained detectable rhythmic expression.

According to recent reports, the composition and temporal profiles of broader rhythmic transcriptional programs also differed between young and aged SCN samples. Aged mice retained detectable circadian rhythms but highlighted reduced 2–6 h ultradian wavelet power in locomotor activity and body temperature, lower activity–temperature correlations, and altered optimal integration windows and time-of-day-dependent relationships. Histological analyses revealed glial remodeling and reduced neuronal marker-positive cell density in the aged SCN.

These findings identify parallel age-associated changes in SCN molecular and cellular organization and in physiological rhythmic power and activity–temperature associations.

  • According to recent reports, biting into a tart lemon bar or sipping a sweet-and-sour beverage delivers a complex blend of chemical stimuli to the tongue simultaneously.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that researchers discovered that taste buds actively process and filter mixed flavors before sending signals to the brain. The study highlights that sour stimuli trigger serotonin release inside taste buds, dampening neural responses to sweet, bitter, and salty flavors while downstream neurons sort tastes into two broad categories: pleasant or unpleasant.

Source: Society for Neuroscience.

According to recent reports, biting into a tart lemon bar or sipping a sweet-and-sour beverage delivers a complex blend of chemical stimuli to the tongue simultaneously. For decades, neuroscientists have worked to determine whether the brain mixes these individual flavor signals centrally, or whether taste buds themselves edit and shape flavor combinations before a single electrical impulse ever leaves the tongue.

In a study published in Journal of Neuroscience, neuroscientists led by Dr. Stephen Roper at the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine recorded gustatory nerve signaling in mice exposed to mixed taste solutions.

The findings reveal that sourness exerts a dominant, suppressive effect over other primary tastes right inside the taste bud, driven by local serotonin signaling.

To trace how mixed tastes travel from peripheral receptors to the central nervous system, Roper and colleagues measured neural responses along the gustatory pathway while exposing mice to single tastes and multi-taste mixtures.

Comparing neural firing across taste conditions revealed two striking principles of gustatory coding:.

To uncover how sourness mutes competing tastes so early in the sensory pipeline, the investigators zeroed in on serotonin, a neurotransmitter released inside each taste bud by specialized sour-responsive receptor cells (Type III taste cells).

Manipulating local serotonin levels directly controlled the strength of flavor suppression:.

These results demonstrate that taste buds function as miniature computational hubs, using paracrine serotonin signaling to inhibit neighboring receptor cells before gustatory information is handed off to cranial nerves.

Sources indicate that “Taste buds not only respond to and transduce taste compounds, they also integrate and manipulate gustatory signals before transmitting them to the brain,” explained Roper. “The neurons that collect signals produced in taste buds are themselves organized into two large groups or clusters, neurons that convey gustatory signals associated with pleasure and neurons that convey unpleasant taste signals.”.

By establishing how peripheral serotonin signaling shapes flavor dominance and how downstream neurons sort palatability, the study lays groundwork for identifying the genetic signatures of pleasure- versus aversion-coding taste neurons, and exploring whether targeted molecular interventions could one day modulate taste perception in clinical nutrition or sensory disorders.

Why do sour flavors overpower sweet, salty, and bitter tastes?

According to recent reports, researchers at the University of Miami found that sour-responsive cells inside taste buds release the neurotransmitter serotonin. This local serotonin dampens the signals of neighboring sweet, bitter, and salty receptor cells before the taste information even reaches the nerves leading to the brain.

Do taste buds simply send raw flavor data to the brain?

It has been revealed that no. The study shows that taste buds act like miniature processing centers that actively mix, filter, and modify taste signals locally before transmitting them to sensory neurons.

How do taste nerves organize flavors on their way to the brain?

According to the researchers, the sensory neurons collecting signals from taste buds are broadly organized into two major functional groups: neurons that carry pleasant taste signals and neurons that carry unpleasant taste signals.

Sour Suppresses Sweet, Salty, and Bitter: Implications for Signal Processing in Taste Buds.

Taste is typically encountered as complex blends, yet how peripheral taste organs process heterogeneous mixtures remains poorly understood. Here we asked how sour stimuli influence the encoding of sweet, salty, and bitter tastes in primary gustatory sensory neurons.

In a recent development, using in vivo calcium imaging in mice of either sex to record neurons in geniculate ganglia during oral delivery of tastants, we compared responses to naturally occurring taste stimuli presented alone versus in binary mixtures that activate acid (sour)-sensing (Type III) taste bud cells. Adding citric acid or HCl robustly suppressed sucrose-evoked responses in geniculate ganglion neurons, even though acid itself did not activate those neurons.

Acid-induced suppression generalized to bitter and salty tastes, which, like sucrose, are believed to activate Type II taste cells. Additional stimuli that activate acid-sensing taste cells (NH4Cl, KCl) also reduced sucrose responses, supporting a common mechanism linked to Type III cells. Manipulating levels of serotonin (a paracrine transmitter released by Type III cells) in taste buds altered taste suppression: increasing serotonin with 5-hydroxytryptophan enhanced acid-induced suppression whereas depleting serotonin with para-chlorophenylalanine weakened it.

Finally, population analyses, including UMAP dimensionality reduction, indicate that taste suppression is not limited to a particular subset of gustatory sensory neurons. The findings are consistent with serotonin-dependent paracrine inhibition within taste buds as a contributor to sour-driven suppression in taste mixtures and reveal a compression of gustatory information into hedonic categories as early as at the level of primary sensory neurons.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Whether ducking a fast-moving ball, stepping back from an oncoming vehicle, or evading an approaching predator, survival depends on the brain’s ability to determine not just that an object is moving, but its exact trajectory in real time.
  • For decades, visual neuroscientists knew that specialized neurons in the mammalian retina fire selectively when stimuli move in specific directions, left, right, up, down, or diagonally.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that researchers have developed a high-throughput brain-mapping tool that reveals the brain does not simply rely on pre-calculated motion signals from the eye, but also computes the direction of movement independently. The study mapped nearly 46,000 mouse brain cells to uncover a dual visual system in the superior colliculus, separating localized object tracking from global self-motion sensing.

Source: UC San Francisco / Nature.

Whether ducking a fast-moving ball, stepping back from an oncoming vehicle, or evading an approaching predator, survival depends on the brain’s ability to determine not just that an object is moving, but its exact trajectory in real time.

For decades, visual neuroscientists knew that specialized neurons in the mammalian retina fire selectively when stimuli move in specific directions, left, right, up, down, or diagonally.

Because these retinal ganglion cells already encode directional vectors, researchers widely assumed the brain simply inherited that pre-calculated motion data passively from the eye. However, no mapping technology existed that could simultaneously trace exact synaptic connections from the retina while identifying the molecular identity of every receiving brain cell.

Now, in a study published in Nature, researchers at UC San Francisco (UCSF) have bridged that technological gap.

Led by co-senior authors Dr. Xin Duan, professor of ophthalmology, and Dr. Evan Feinberg, professor of anatomy, alongside postdoctoral fellow Dr. Fei Wang, the team built a scalable eye-to-brain wiring atlas revealing that specialized circuits in the midbrain compute motion direction completely on their own.

Over the past decade, Duan’s laboratory pioneered anterograde trans-neuronal tracing, a technique in which a fluorescent molecular tracer delivered to the eye crosses synaptic junctions to illuminate only those downstream brain neurons directly receiving retinal input.

To scale this tool from single-circuit tracing into a comprehensive atlas, Wang paired the trans-neuronal tracer with MERFISH (multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization), a spatial transcriptomic method that reads gene activity across thousands of individual cells in a tissue slice simultaneously to pinpoint each neuron’s exact genetic identity.

Applying this combined platform across nearly 46,000 cells in the mouse visual system, the investigators uncovered hundreds of distinct retinal-to-brain connection pairs.

“It’s like an entire atlas we’ve built,” Wang noted. “We’ve uncovered hundreds of pairs of connections between the eye and the brain. We ended up focusing on only one page of this atlas, but there are many left to study in the future.”.

Focusing on the superior colliculus, an evolutionarily conserved midbrain hub essential for visual orientation and rapid motor reflexes, Wang, Feinberg, and Duan recorded real-time neural firing while showing mice high-contrast black bars scrolling across a screen in eight distinct directions.

Combining functional recordings with their molecular wiring map exposed two separate motion-processing architectures operating side by side:.

Sources indicate that “We think these sets of cells are doing slightly different things from each other,” Wang explained. “The eye cells detecting direction may specialize in small, local motions like prey or food. The brain cells computing direction sense a larger background movement.”.

The investigators hypothesize that this global background motion signal informs an organism of its own self-motion and spatial trajectory as it navigates through the environment.

Recent findings suggest that beyond resolving a foundational question in visual neuroscience, the high-resolution wiring atlas carries direct translational implications for regenerative medicine and neuroengineering. As researchers advance toward optic nerve regeneration, whole-eye transplantation, and high-resolution visual brain-machine interfaces for patients with glaucoma, trauma, or multiple sclerosis, restoring functional sight requires reconnecting damaged axons to their exact functional targets.

“This is a fundamental mechanism that has been understudied from a basic science perspective, but it also has applied value,” said Duan. “If we ever want to repair or restore vision in people, we need to know which neural connections need to be rewired for functional vision.”.

“In addition to providing a blueprint for revealing structural maps of the brain, our study illustrates how the resulting maps can be used to answer longstanding questions regarding brain function,” added Feinberg.

The team notes that their scalable tracer-plus-MERFISH platform can be adapted to map how the eye regulates circadian rhythms, and generalized to chart cell-to-cell connectivity across any organ system in the body.

Does the eye do all the work of detecting which way things move?

No. While specialized cells in the retina detect motion direction and send that data to the brain, UCSF researchers discovered a second group of neurons in the brain’s superior colliculus that independently calculates motion direction using basic visual inputs, even when the eye’s own direction-sensing cells are turned off.

Why does the brain have two different systems for sensing motion?

Researchers believe the two pathways handle different visual jobs: the eye’s direction-sensing cells appear specialized for tracking small, local moving targets (like food, prey, or a flying ball), while the brain’s independent motion-computing cells detect large-scale background movement to help track how your own body is moving through space.

How could this brain-mapping tool help restore vision in the future?

To successfully develop eye transplants, optic nerve repairs, or visual brain-machine interfaces for conditions like glaucoma or multiple sclerosis, scientists need an exact wiring diagram showing which eye cells connect to which functional brain circuits. This upcoming atlas provides that precise rewiring blueprint.

TransA-MERFISH reveals divergent post-retinal direction-selective circuits.

A major goal in neuroscience is to map the transformation of information as it flows through the brain. For example, neurons at many levels of the visual hierarchy are attuned to motion direction. However, links between motion-selective computations and cell types at various stages of the visual hierarchy remain unidentified. A key first step in delineating these relationships is to map the wiring diagrams that connect different motion-selective cell types.

Here we establish a systematic, cell-type-specific circuit-mapping method, combining an anterograde trans-neuronal fluorescent tracer (mWGA–mCherry) with spatial transcriptomics (multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (MERFISH)) to establish TransA-MERFISH. We used TransA-MERFISH to comprehensively map the synaptic target cell types of four retinal ganglion cell subclasses in superior colliculus (SC) at cell-type resolution.

These experiments unexpectedly revealed that retinal on–off direction-selective ganglion cells (ooDSGCs) innervate several direction-selective SC cell types, but do not innervate a SC cell type that was previously reported to display strong direction-selective responses.

We validated these results using orthogonal approaches and demonstrated the sensitivity and specificity of TransA-MERFISH. Functional studies of SC activity before and after ablation of retinal direction-selective circuits confirmed that these computationally distinct, ooDSGC-dependent and -independent direction-selective cell types are commingled in SC.

Together, our study establishes TransA-MERFISH as a robust framework for mapping wiring diagrams at the cell-type level and uncovers divergent computational mechanisms of motion detection in early visual processing.

Ultraprocessed Foods Alter Food-Reward Brain Activity

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A controlled feeding trial reveals that just two weeks on a diet high in ultraprocessed foods alters brain reward responses in emerging adults ages 18 to 21, while leaving adults ages 22 to 25 unaffected.
  • Ultraprocessed foods, products formulated with industrial processing methods and ingredients rarely found in a home kitchen, account for more than half of the calories consumed by young adults in the United States.
  • In a controlled feeding study published this month in the journal Obesity, researchers at Virginia Tech’s Fralin Biomedical Research Institute at VTC and Department of Human Nutrition, Foods, and Exercise found that emerging adults ages 18 to 21 exhibit distinct neural changes in food-reward circuitry after consuming an ultraprocessed diet for just two weeks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A controlled feeding trial reveals that just two weeks on a diet high in ultraprocessed foods alters brain reward responses in emerging adults ages 18 to 21, while leaving adults ages 22 to 25 unaffected. The fMRI study indicates blunted activation in the developing orbitofrontal cortex, a key region for food valuation and self-control, even when diets are strictly matched for calories, sugar, fat, and nutrients.

Source: Virginia Tech / Obesity.

Ultraprocessed foods, products formulated with industrial processing methods and ingredients rarely found in a home kitchen, account for more than half of the calories consumed by young adults in the United States. While extensive research links these foods to obesity, metabolic syndrome, and cardiovascular disease, neuroscientists are increasingly uncovering how industrial processing directly interacts with the developing human brain.

In a controlled feeding study published this month in the journal Obesity, researchers at Virginia Tech’s Fralin Biomedical Research Institute at VTC and Department of Human Nutrition, Foods, and Exercise found that emerging adults ages 18 to 21 exhibit distinct neural changes in food-reward circuitry after consuming an ultraprocessed diet for just two weeks.

Led by first author Dr. Emma Leslie alongside neuroscientist Dr. Alex DiFeliceantonio and registered dietitian Dr. Brenda Davy, the findings complement earlier results from the same trial showing that 18- to 21-year-olds consumed excess calories at a buffet meal after eating ultraprocessed foods, even when they were no longer hungry.

To separate the effects of industrial food processing from basic nutritional content, the researchers recruited 22 healthy adults ages 18 to 25 (including seven participants ages 21 or younger) for a randomized crossover feeding trial. Each participant followed two strictly controlled diets for two weeks apiece, separated by a four-week washout period:.

Critically, both diets were engineered to have identical macronutrient profiles (50% carbohydrates, 35% fat, 15% protein), matching levels of fiber, added sugars, saturated fat, sodium, energy density, and overall nutritional quality, calibrated to keep each participant’s body weight stable.

Before and after each two-week dietary phase, participants underwent functional MRI (fMRI) brain scans while receiving small sips of an ultraprocessed milkshake or a tasteless control solution through a specialized delivery tube.

When the researchers analyzed the neuroimaging data, they discovered a striking developmental divide:.

“Among the younger participants, consuming a diet high in ultraprocessed foods for just two weeks was associated with decreased brain response to a rewarding food — a milkshake — in the orbitofrontal cortex,” explained Leslie, who conducted the work as a doctoral student at Virginia Tech and is now a postdoctoral associate at the University of Michigan.

In a recent development, located just behind the eyes, the orbitofrontal cortex is one of the final regions of the human brain to finish maturing, continuing to remodel into the mid- to late 20s. It plays a central role in evaluating food rewards, regulating cravings, and exerting executive self-control to stop eating.

Because the two diets were matched across nutritional metrics, the findings point toward non-nutritive properties of ultraprocessed foods, such as chemical additives, emulsifiers, texture alterations, or compounds generated during industrial processing, as potential drivers of altered brain signaling.

Sources indicate that “This study is important because you have this change in an area of the brain known to govern self-control and potentially put a stop to eating,” said DiFeliceantonio, associate professor at the Fralin Biomedical Research Institute and interim co-director of its Center for Health Behaviors Research. “This is giving us insight into how ultraprocessed foods are affecting the bodies and brains of younger people, who might be especially vulnerable to their effects. And that’s important to know for things like dietary guidelines, doctor recommendations, and policy decisions.”.

While the researchers note that the sample size was small and the age-based findings were exploratory, and did not directly correlate individual fMRI shifts with buffet calorie intake, the results highlight adolescence and early adulthood as critical windows of neurodevelopmental sensitivity.

Next, DiFeliceantonio and Davy plan to investigate whether adolescents under 18, who consume the highest proportion of ultraprocessed foods of any U.S. demographic, show even stronger neural sensitivity, and whether brain responses recover once individuals return to whole-food diets.

How do ultraprocessed foods affect the brains of young adults?

Sources indicate that A Virginia Tech study found that after eating a diet high in ultraprocessed foods for just two weeks, young adults ages 18 to 21 highlighted decreased brain activity in the orbitofrontal cortex, a region involved in food reward, valuation, and self-control, when tasting a milkshake. Adults ages 22 to 25 did not show these brain changes.

Was the brain effect simply caused by extra sugar, fat, or calories?

No. Both the ultraprocessed diet and the unprocessed comparison diet contained the exact same amounts of calories, carbohydrates, fat, protein, added sugars, saturated fat, fiber, and sodium. This suggests that industrial food processing or additives themselves, rather than basic nutrients, drove the brain changes.

Why are 18- to 21-year-olds more sensitive to ultraprocessed foods than slightly older adults?

Industry observers note that the orbitofrontal cortex is one of the last brain regions to finish developing, continuing to mature into the mid- to late 20s. Because this self-control and reward-evaluation circuit is still actively wiring in 18- to 21-year-olds, it appears more sensitive to dietary shifts.

Funding: The research was supported by a grant to DiFeliceantonio and Davy from the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, part of the National Institutes of Health. Leslie was also supported with an exercise health sciences graduate fellowship from Dr. Ray A. Gaskins.

The average American consumes 55% of daily energy from ultraprocessed foods (UPF), created through industrial processes and additives not used at home. We investigated if a high-UPF diet alters brain response to milkshake compared with a diet free from UPF in emerging adults, who are in a critical brain development period and typically consume high amounts of UPF.

Recent findings suggest that in a randomized controlled crossover trial participants aged 18–25 years completed two 2-week controlled feeding periods including a UPF (81% UPF) and non-UPF (0% UPF) diet. Before and after each diet intervention, participants consumed milkshake concomitant with functional magnetic resonance imaging.

Recent findings suggest that in the entire cohort, there were no differences between diet conditions in brain response. An exploratory analysis revealed orbitofrontal cortex response to milkshake decreased after the UPF diet and increased following the non-UPF diet in late adolescents (18–21 years) but not young adults (22–25 years). In all participants, habitual UPF intake (g) was positively associated with orbitofrontal cortex response to milkshake, independent of diet condition.

It has been revealed that an acute UPF dietary intervention may only alter brain response in late adolescents. Further work is needed to determine potential vulnerability of late adolescents to changes in dietary UPF on brain response to rewards.

ClinicalTrials.gov identifier NCT05550818.

Tech Report: Intolerance of Uncertainty Surged 3x Faster Since 2012

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1385 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A large-scale meta-analysi reveals that intolerance of uncertainty, a core cognitive driver of clinical anxiety, has climbed steadily among North American college students since 1992, accelerating threefold faster after 2012.
  • Source: Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.
  • According to recent reports, over the past decade, rates of anxiety and mood disorders among adolescents and college-aged adults have climbed sharply across North America.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A large-scale meta-analysi reveals that intolerance of uncertainty, a core cognitive driver of clinical anxiety, has climbed steadily among North American college students since 1992, accelerating threefold faster after 2012. The analysis of over 35,000 participants indicates that rising youth anxiety reflects genuine shifts in psychological distress rather than mere mental health awareness.

Source: Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.

According to recent reports, over the past decade, rates of anxiety and mood disorders among adolescents and college-aged adults have climbed sharply across North America. Yet clinicians and epidemiologists have hotly debated a central question: does this statistical surge reflect a true rise in underlying psychological distress, or are young people simply more familiar with clinical terminology and more willing to report symptoms?

New research led by Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health and Boston University School of Public Health provides compelling evidence that underlying cognitive vulnerability is genuinely intensifying.

Published in JAMA Psychiatry, the study tracks three decades of data on intolerance of uncertainty (IU)—a foundational psychological mechanism characterized by acute distress when facing ambiguous situations, missing information, or unpredictable outcomes.

Analyzing data from more than 35,000 college students in the United States and Canada between 1992 and 2023, the researchers found that intolerance of uncertainty increased steadily over 30 years—and accelerated dramatically around 2012, growing roughly three times faster over the past decade than during the 1990s and 2000s.

According to recent reports, to track population-level shifts in how young adults tolerate ambiguity, first author Dr. Jeroen M. Van Baar, postdoctoral associate in epidemiology at Boston University School of Public Health, and senior author Dr. Katherine M. Keyes, professor of epidemiology at Columbia Mailman School of Public Health, conducted a systematic temporal meta-analysis using the Web of Science database.

After screening nearly 300 full-text peer-reviewed studies published between 2007 and 2025, the team synthesized data from 138 studies encompassing 35,296 college-aged participants across the U.S. and Canada who completed standardized 27-item or 12-item versions of the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale.

Across the entire 31-year window from 1992 through 2023, average IU scores increased by approximately 0.65 points annually. Crucially, the trajectory bent sharply upward around 2012: between 2012 and 2023, intolerance of uncertainty rose at roughly triple the annual pace recorded between 1992 and 2011.

“Our results provide updated insights into one of the core building blocks of anxiety: intolerance of uncertainty,” explained Keyes. “IU is not itself a health outcome or a root cause of disease, but an intermediary cognitive process that contributes to the development of anxiety.”.

For an individual with high intolerance of uncertainty, everyday unpredictability, such as attending a new class without knowing every expectation or navigating an unstructured social event, can trigger disproportionate cognitive threat and emotional distress. Elevated IU is a well-established transdiagnostic risk factor linked to generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and depression.

Crucially, because “intolerance of uncertainty” remains a specialized clinical metric largely unfamiliar outside psychology, it provides a vital safeguard against reporting bias.

“Some researchers have argued that increases in anxiety and mood disorder symptoms among young people may partly reflect greater mental health awareness,” noted Van Baar. “Because young people are now more familiar with terms like ‘anxiety’, they may be more likely to report symptoms in surveys even if their underlying feelings have not changed. On the other hand, intolerance of uncertainty remains a relatively unfamiliar concept outside psychology, making this study less vulnerable to that criticism.”.

“The fact that we observed a consistent increase in intolerance of uncertainty that mirrored trends in anxiety and mood disorder symptoms suggests these patterns are unlikely to be explained solely by greater mental health awareness and may instead reflect genuine changes in underlying mental health,” Keyes added.

While the study did not isolate a single environmental trigger, the authors point to a convergence of mutually reinforcing societal shifts—including the rapid adoption of smartphones and social media around 2012, escalating academic competition, rising loneliness, economic instability, childhood adversity, and the COVID-19 pandemic.

“It is likely that these factors are intertwined and mutually reinforcing, jointly contributing to population-level increases in intolerance of uncertainty and anxiety among young adults,” Van Baar noted. “Any explanation will be strongest if it accounts for both the long-term upward trend since the 1990s and the inflection point observed around 2012.”.

Despite the sobering trajectory, the researchers emphasize a clear path forward: unlike broad macroeconomic forces, intolerance of uncertainty is a modifiable cognitive habit. Targeted cognitive-behavioral therapies specifically designed to build tolerance for ambiguity already exist, and scaling these interventions for young adults could help curb the youth anxiety crisis at its cognitive roots.

What is “intolerance of uncertainty,” and how does it relate to anxiety?

Intolerance of uncertainty is a psychological tendency to feel distressed, overwhelmed, or threatened when facing unpredictable outcomes or missing information. It acts as a core cognitive building block that significantly increases a person’s vulnerability to developing anxiety and mood disorders.

How much has intolerance of uncertainty increased among college students?

Analyzing data from 35,296 U.S. and Canadian college students between 1992 and 2023, researchers found that scores rose steadily by about 0.65 points per year, and accelerated three times faster between 2012 and 2023 compared to the previous two decades.

Does this prove rising youth anxiety isn’t just due to greater mental health awareness?

Yes, it provides strong evidence against the “awareness-only” theory. Because “intolerance of uncertainty” is a specialized psychological concept rather than an everyday term young people use to self-label, its steep rise mirrors anxiety trends without being skewed by changing vocabulary or awareness.

Funding: The study was supported by the National Institute of Mental Health, grant 5T32MH013043.The authors have no financial conflicts of interest to declare.

Recent findings suggest that intolerance of Uncertainty among U.S. and Canadian Young Adults Attending College 1992-2023: A Meta-analysis.

Recent findings suggest that rising anxiety prevalence among young adults may relate to intolerance of uncertainty (IU), difficulty enduring the perceived absence of vital information. A prior meta-analysis found increasing long-form Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IUS) scores among US and Canadian undergraduates from 1992 to 2014, but recent evidence is lacking.

To estimate IU trends among US and Canadian young adults attending college 1992-2023 by extending the prior meta-analysis and including the short-form IUS.

Web of Science was used to track English-language articles from Canada or the US citing the source articles for the long-form or short-form IUS across 13 databases.

Eligible studies were peer-reviewed empirical articles with nonclinical undergraduate samples from the US or Canada that reported sample size and mean long-form or short-form IUS.

Recent findings suggest that following MOOSE guidelines, 2 investigators extracted study characteristics and mean IU, resolving discrepancies jointly. Studies were merged with the prior meta-analysis and analyzed using fixed-effect meta-regression. To assess IU across scale forms, mean IU was converted into SD units and regressed onto data collection year, weighted by sample size, and adjusted for mean age and sex or gender distribution. Study data were analyzed from September 2025 to July 2026.

Mean IU. The hypothesis was preregistered before data collection.

Sources indicate that of 799 abstracts screened and 294 full texts reviewed independently by 2 investigators, 92 articles (11%) met selection criteria. After merger with prior meta-analysis and removal of duplicates, this meta-analysis included 137 studies (62 long-form IUS and 75 short-form IUS) comprising 37 298 participants (unweighted median [IQR] of sample mean age, 20.1 [19.4-21.3] years; 69.5% female [unweighted mean of sample sex/gender distribution]). Mean long-form IU increased from 1992 to 2023 by 0.66 points annually (95% CI, 0.47-0.84 points) on a scale from 27 to 135. Mean short-form IU increased from 2005 (first sample) to 2023 by 0.60 points annually (95% CI, 0.43-0.76 points) on a scale from 12 to 60. In the combined sample, mean IU grew by 0.04 SD per year from 1992 to 2023 (95% CI, 0.03-0.05 SD per year), with 3-fold faster growth during 2012-2023 (0.06 SD per year; 95% CI, 0.04-0.08 SD per year) than during 1992-2011 (0.02 SD per year; 95% CI, 0-0.04 SD per year).

According to recent reports, results of this meta-analysis suggest that IU increased among US and Canadian young adults attending college 1992-2023, with a steeper increase after 2012. This supports further investigating the role of uncertainty in the epidemiology of anxiety.

Reduce your belly fat 10 percent with a half cup of this food.

Lowering sugar consumption by about one can of soda and adding one half-cup of fibre-rich foods daily reduces abdominal fat and type 2 diabetes risk.

A study has found that decreasing about 47 grams of sugar intake per day — equivalent to a can of soda — lowers insulin secretion, on average, by 33 percent.

Increasing fibre intake by 5 grams a day — the amount in a half cup of beans — results in a 10 percent reduction of belly fat.

Visceral fat is a type of body fat stored within the abdominal area and internal organs.

This type of fat causes abdominal obesity and is also associated with several health problems, like type 2 diabetes, heart disease, and cancer.

Dr Emily Ventura and colleagues conducted a 16-week study on overweight Latino adolescents who were between 12 to 19 years old.

They tested if increasing fiber consumption and decreasing sugar intake have an effect on type 2 diabetes risk factors.

“A reduction in visceral fat indicates a reduction in risk for type 2 diabetes, considering that to a greater degree than total body fat, visceral fat [fat surrounding the internal organs] has been shown to be negatively associated with insulin sensitivity.”.

It has been revealed that those who increased fiber intake had a significant reduction in body mass index (-2 percent vs. 2 percent) and visceral adipose tissue (-10 percent vs. no change) compared with those who decreased fiber intake.”.

Being overweight or obese are serious complications affecting adults and children around the world.

The World Health Organization reports that in 2016 over 1.9 billion adults were overweight and more than 650 million adults were obese.

The authors of this study wrote:.

“Our results suggest that intensive interventions may not be necessary to achieve modifications in sugar and fiber intake.

Accordingly, nutritional guidance given in the primary care or community setting may be sufficient to promote the suggested dietary changes in some individuals.

In addition, policies that promote reduced intake of added sugar and increased intake of fiber could be effective public health strategies for the prevention of type 2 diabetes in this high-risk population.”.

The study was published in the Archives of Pediatrics and Adolescent Medicine (Ventura et al., 2009).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the Academy of Natural Sciences, a 198-year-old public museum in Philadelphia run by Drexel University, shuttered in September because of rising costs. The university’s president will now testify under subpoena before Philadelphia’s city council on 16 November, answering questions about the sudden closure and what will happen to the museum’s valuable collection of more than 19 million specimens.

While many of the Academy’s workers have been laid off, collection managers still on staff have faced an “astronomical increase” in emails and calls, states Amber Redfield, a former geosciences collection manager and fossil preparator at the Academy who was recently laid off and is now volunteering there. She says that people have been asking: “Is this safe?” “Can I see it?” “Can I book an appointment?”.

Isa Betancourt, a former curatorial assistant in the entomology department and an organiser with the Save the Academy coalition, states the number of curators has dropped from 11 to five. The invertebrate palaeontology collection manager recently left for a job at the American Museum of Natural History. “There is no strategy to replace her," Betancourt tells The Art Newspaper. Endowed curator posts in entomology and palaeontology have gone unfilled for years, she adds.

It has been revealed that founded in 1812, the Academy describes itself as the oldest natural history research institution in the Americas. It opened its museum to the public in 1828 and, in 1868, put Hadrosaurus foulkii on view as the world’s first mounted dinosaur skeleton. Its millions of specimens include plants collected on the Lewis and Clark expedition, John James Audubon’s birds and Thomas Jefferson’s fossils.

Sources indicate that the Academy became a Drexel affiliate in 2011, while retaining its status as a separate non-profit with its own board. Drexel recently told the city council it had “stepped in as a partner” that year, when the Academy “faced severe financial distress”.

According to recent reports, the city council passed a resolution on 17 September to investigate the Academy’s closing. The resolution calls institutions like the Academy “part of the cultural fabric of the city” and states its shuttering would especially affect area residents “for whom the museum is a fixture of the neighbourhood”. An initial hearing took place on 26 October, which Drexel’s president did not attend.

At the hearing, representatives for Drexel cited the building's "substantial capital needs" and told the city council that public exhibitions need a upcoming model, "almost certainly in a different location".

Recent findings suggest that sarah McAnulty, a squid biologist and Save the Academy organiser, states city council members asked Drexel representatives to check their numbers. "If all you need to keep the public museum open is a million dollars, what the hell are we doing here?" she says, describing the city council’s reaction.

The Academy’s Dinosaur Hall Photo: Ms3733, via Wikimedia Commons.

According to recent reports, staff learned of the Academy’s closure at a morning meeting on 1 September, Redfield notes. Most staff were laid off by 1 November, and many people "found out they were let go in a report by The Philadelphia Inquirer", she adds.

Redfield says the museum drew more than 60,000 visitors in its final 12 days of public hours. "That's not enough time to shut down a lifetime of scientific and educational work," she adds. "I planned to retire at the Academy and don't have any backup looks." Now she is volunteering.

Sources indicate that "Unfortunately, volunteer labour is essential to most natural history collections, but it’s not sustainable,” Betancourt indicates. “The fact that the volunteer manager was initially slated for termination and had to be reinstated indicates Drexel has no idea how these collections function.".

Betancourt adds that the Academy's social media accounts have been inactive for two months and staff do not have access because Drexel controls them. The Academy's director of marketing and communications was let go with the closure. Betancourt says the university may not realise that communications and education staff connect the collections with the public and potential benefactors, "otherwise, the collections work in darkness”.

The William Penn Foundation has offered a year of funding to replace Drexel's subsidy for the museum. "The foundation has not received a response to our offer," a spokesperson told the Inquirer. Drexel later stated that it had not received a "formal proposal with a defined level of financial support".

Betancourt indicates Save the Academy wants Drexel to explain "why no capital campaign was undertaken" and "why the scientific community has been shut out of behind-the-scenes negotiations. The closed-door negotiations got us a closed museum. Natural history collections tied to a financially haemorrhaging university are not safe natural history collections.”.

Breaking: Losing a Single “Molecular Brake” Gene Triggers Brain Overgrowth

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (919 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers mapped the cellular domino effect triggered when developing brain stem cells lose the Pten gene.
  • Source: Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) / Science Advances.
  • Building a functional human cerebral cortex requires extraordinary cellular precision: neural stem cells must divide, differentiate, and stop growing on a strict developmental schedule so that billions of neurons and glial cells assemble in exact proportions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers mapped the cellular domino effect triggered when developing brain stem cells lose the Pten gene. The single-cell lineage-tracing study reveals that individual neural progenitors lacking Pten generate 25% more neurons alongside an excess of enlarged astrocytes, and reroute glial cell production through the MAPK pathway, offering a potential upcoming target for drug-resistant brain tumors.

Source: Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) / Science Advances.

Building a functional human cerebral cortex requires extraordinary cellular precision: neural stem cells must divide, differentiate, and stop growing on a strict developmental schedule so that billions of neurons and glial cells assemble in exact proportions.

Acting as a vital molecular brake during this process is the Pten gene, which restrains cell division and keeps tissue growth balanced.

Industry observers note that when mutations disable PTEN, that biological brake fails. Individuals carrying PTEN mutations frequently develop megalencephaly, an unusually enlarged brain, alongside elevated rates of autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, epilepsy, and brain tumors, a constellation of symptoms known clinically as PTEN Hamartoma Tumor Syndrome.

Now, in a study published in Science Advances, the Hippenmeyer group at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA), collaborating with researchers at Sorbonne Université in Paris, Yale School of Medicine, and Vetmeduni Vienna, has traced the exact single-cell chain reaction unleashed when Pten is lost in developing brain stem cells.

Because switching off Pten across the entire brain causes severe early lethality in animal models, isolating how the mutation alters individual stem cell behavior has historically been difficult.

To overcome this hurdle, first author Dr. Osvaldo Miranda Romero, a postdoctoral researcher in Simon Hippenmeyer’s laboratory at ISTA, utilized Mosaic Analysis with Double Markers (MADM), a high-precision genetic lineage-tracing technique that deletes Pten in only a tiny, sparse fraction of cortical radial glial stem cells while tagging them and all their descendants with bright fluorescent markers.

“Until now, we lacked basic information about what Pten mutations mean at the level of individual cells and how they affect cellular output, in other words, the quantity and identity of cells produced from stem cells,” explained Romero.

Tracking these fluorescent cellular family trees across mouse brain development revealed a twofold driver of brain overgrowth:.

To uncover how Pten loss forces stem cells to overproduce astrocytes, the team investigated the intracellular signaling pathways governing glial differentiation. Under typical developmental conditions, radial glial progenitors depend on the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) pathway to transition into astrocytes.

However, when Romero and colleagues simultaneously switched off both Pten and Egfr in individual radial glial cells, astrocyte overproduction continued unabated. Molecular analysis revealed that Pten-deficient progenitors had completely bypassed the standard EGFR route, rerouting glial differentiation through an alternative signaling cascade: the MAPK pathway.

“Under normal conditions, EGFR is an important driver of glial-cell formation, whereas MAPK can serve as a kind of alternative route under exceptional circumstances,” Romero noted.

Beyond illuminating the developmental origins of autism and megalencephaly, this signaling detour carries direct implications for neuro-oncology. Patients with PTEN mutations face a heightened risk of developing gliomas, aggressive brain tumors composed of astrocytes and other glial cells.

Recent findings suggest that clinicians frequently treat gliomas with drugs designed to block EGFR signaling, yet many patients eventually develop treatment resistance. By demonstrating that Pten loss allows glial cells to sidestep EGFR via MAPK activation, the study highlights a promising therapeutic target.

“Our findings suggest that the MAPK signaling pathway could be investigated as a potential therapeutic target in such cases in the future,” Romero concluded.

How does losing the Pten gene lead to an unusually large brain (megalencephaly)?

Industry observers note that researchers at ISTA found that when individual brain stem cells (radial glia) lack the Pten gene, they lose their natural growth brake, producing about 25% more neurons and significantly more astrocytes than normal. Both the neurons and astrocytes also grow abnormally large, expanding overall brain tissue volume.

What conditions are linked to PTEN mutations in humans?

Mutations in PTEN are associated with PTEN Hamartoma Tumor Syndrome, which increases the likelihood of megalencephaly (enlarged brain size), autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disability, epilepsy, and glial brain tumors called gliomas.

How could this discovery help treat brain tumors in the future?

Glial brain tumors are often treated with drugs that block the EGFR signaling pathway, but tumors frequently become resistant. Researchers discovered that cells missing Pten bypass EGFR by switching to the alternative MAPK pathway to make astrocytes—suggesting that targeting MAPK could help overcome drug resistance.

Pten Regulates Neurogenic Radial Glia Lineage Progression and Tunes Neocortical Astrocyte Production in Mapk1/3-dependent Pathway.

Industry observers note that the cerebral cortex consists of immense numbers of diverse cell types derived from radial glial progenitor (RGP) cells. How RGPs generate appropriate quantities of distinct cell types to safeguard a brain of correct size is not well understood. However, genetic aberrations in human, including mutations in PTEN, lead to cortical malformation such as macrocephaly, albeit with unknown etiology.

Here, we used mosaic analysis with double markers (MADM)–based clonal analysis and single-cell phenotyping to decipher the role of Pten in RGP lineage progression during cortical ontogeny. Although neurogenic RGP lineage progression was altered and projection neuron production doubled in the absence of Pten, cortical astrogenesis was drastically increased. Through epistasis experiments, we show that the loss of Pten uncouples astrogenesis from essential growth factor signaling hubs, funneling into MAPK (mitogen-activated protein kinase).

Collectively, our results suggest that Pten regulates RGP lineage progression with distinct sequential functions in corticogenesis to safeguard the emergence of a correctly sized cortex.

Screen Time and Fitness Reshape Grey Matter in Teen Brains

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A neuroimaging study reveals that daily screen time, physical activity, and physical fitness leave distinct structural signatures on the developing adolescent brain.
  • In a recent development, adolescence is a period of profound structural remodeling in the human brain.
  • At the same time, modern teenagers navigate unprecedented daily exposure to smartphones, gaming, and digital media alongside wide variations in physical exercise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A neuroimaging study reveals that daily screen time, physical activity, and physical fitness leave distinct structural signatures on the developing adolescent brain. Using MRI scans of teenagers aged 16 to 19, researchers found that heavy smart-device usage is associated with reduced grey matter volume in memory-related medial temporal regions alongside altered maturation patterns in frontal and visual cortices.

Source: University of Eastern Finland.

In a recent development, adolescence is a period of profound structural remodeling in the human brain. Throughout the late teenage years, neural circuits undergo a natural fine-tuning process known as synaptic pruning—trimming away redundant connections to streamline communication, boost processing efficiency, and sharpen executive control.

At the same time, modern teenagers navigate unprecedented daily exposure to smartphones, gaming, and digital media alongside wide variations in physical exercise.

In a neuroimaging investigation conducted at the University of Eastern Finland and Kuopio University Hospital, researchers examined how these everyday lifestyle factors correspond to physical differences in adolescent brain structure.

Led by Doctoral Researcher Hannamari Skog of the Institute of Biomedicine, the study evaluated 44 healthy adolescents aged 16 to 19 (25 girls and 19 boys) drawn from the Physical Activity and Nutrition in Children (PANIC) study and the FitBrain cohort.

Using high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to quantify regional grey matter volume alongside validated lifestyle questionnaires and physical fitness testing (including 50-meter shuttle runs and standing long jumps), the researchers uncovered distinct anatomical patterns tied to digital media habits:.

“Excessive screen time and smart device usage may be harmful to the areas of the brain that are involved in memory and learning,” explained Skog.

According to recent reports, however, Skog noted that larger grey matter volume in visual and executive regions during late adolescence is not necessarily advantageous. Because typical teenage brain maturation involves a healthy reduction in grey matter as neural circuits specialize and become more efficient, persistent volume increases in frontal and occipital areas could signal either intensive visual-motor stimulation from apps and games or a developmental delay in cortical pruning.

“The larger volume in these areas may be particularly related to applications and games that require attention, motor planning and visual information processing,” Skog noted. “During normal brain development in adolescence, there is a reduction in grey matter volume and an increase in brain efficiency. The positive link between screen time and the volume of grey matter in these areas may thus also reflect a delay in brain development.”.

Movement and cardiovascular-muscular fitness were also reflected across multiple cortical and subcortical regions:.

Because the study relied on a cross-sectional snapshot of 44 adolescents, the authors emphasize that causal relationships and long-term cognitive outcomes require longitudinal follow-up across adulthood.

Recent findings suggest that “The results provide fresh information on how everyday lifestyle factors, such as screen time, physical activity and physical fitness, are linked to brain structure in adolescence,” Skog concluded. “However, in light of the results, the connections between lifestyle factors and brain structures in adolescence are complex, and more research is needed to understand their long-term significance.”.

How does heavy screen time affect the teenage brain’s structure?

MRI scans from the University of Eastern Finland show that adolescents with high leisure screen time have smaller grey matter volumes in the medial temporal lobe (critical for memory and learning), alongside larger grey matter volumes in frontal and visual regions, which may reflect either heavy visual-motor gaming demands or a delay in normal adolescent brain pruning.

Why can larger grey matter volume in teenagers sometimes indicate delayed brain development?

During healthy adolescence, the brain naturally trims away excess grey matter through synaptic pruning to become faster and more efficient. Having unusually large grey matter volumes in frontal decision-making areas during late adolescence can therefore indicate that this natural maturational streamlining is running behind schedule.

How did physical activity and fitness affect brain volume in this study?

Higher overall physical activity was linked to larger volume in the right visual (occipital) cortex, while better physical fitness scores were associated with larger parietal lobe volume (involved in attention and spatial perception) and smaller volumes in the hippocampus and posterior cingulate gyrus.

Associations of screen time, physical activity and neuromuscular fitness with brain structure in adolescents.

To explore the associations of total screen time, smart device use, physical activity, and neuromuscular fitness with brain gray matter volumes in adolescence.

It has been revealed that brain gray matter volumes were assessed using magnetic resonance imaging in 44 healthy adolescents (25 females and 19 males) aged 16–19 years. Physical activity and sedentary behavior questionnaires were used to assess screen time, including smart device use, and physical activity, including organized sports in sports clubs. Neuromuscular fitness was assessed using a score combining results of a 50-m shuttle-run test and a standing long jump test.

Screen time and smart device use were negatively associated with medial temporal lobe volumes but positively associated with supplementary motor cortex and dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex volumes. Screen time was also positively related to left cuneus volume. Total physical activity was positively associated with right inferior occipital gyrus volume, but the association did not remain statistically significant after correction for multiple testing. Neuromuscular fitness was positively associated with parietal lobe volumes but negatively associated with right hippocampus and left posterior cingulate gyrus volumes, but these associations were no longer statistically significant after correction for multiple testing.

It has been revealed that longer screen time was related to lower medial temporal lobe volumes and larger frontal lobe volumes, whereas higher physical activity and better neuromuscular fitness were associated with larger volumes in the parietal and occipital regions. These findings highlight the complex relationships of screen time and physical activity with brain gray matter volumes in adolescence.

People with a vitamin B12 deficiency are three times more likely to be experiencing ‘melancholic’ depression.

Some of the other most common symptoms of depression are decreased interest in life or pleasure, energy loss and concentration problems.

The study also found a link between low folate intake and depression.

Folates include vitamin B9, folacin and folic acid.

People with a low intake of folates were 50 percent more likely to be experiencing melancholic depression.

The research included 2,806 Finnish people whose nutritional status and depression symptoms were assessed.

Although vitamin B12 and folates were linked to melancholic depression, the same link was not seen with non-melancholic depression.

Vitamin B12 deficiency is easy to rectify with supplements or by dietary changes.

The body uses vitamin B12 to make red blood cells and to keep the nervous system healthy.

Other common signs of vitamin B12 deficiency include experiencing muscle weakness and being constipated.

Meanwhile, some of the best dietary sources of folates include:.

Folate levels are particularly high in chickpeas, yeast extract, lentils and broad beans.

Brain’s Insula Shapes Pain, Emotion, and the Placebo Effect

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (865 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An international team of neuroscientists has mapped the functional architecture of the human insular cortex for the first time, revealing that it operates through four distinct yet cooperating subregions rather than as a passive sensory relay.
  • Source: Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (HHU).
  • It has been revealed that tucked deep within the lateral sulcus beneath the folds of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes lies the insular cortex, or insula, one of the human brain’s most enigmatic hubs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An international team of neuroscientists has mapped the functional architecture of the human insular cortex for the first time, revealing that it operates through four distinct yet cooperating subregions rather than as a passive sensory relay. Drawing on 15 years of direct intracranial brain recordings across 87 epilepsy patients, the researchers uncovered a hierarchical network explaining how emotions and expectations actively reshape physical pain.

Source: Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (HHU).

It has been revealed that tucked deep within the lateral sulcus beneath the folds of the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes lies the insular cortex, or insula, one of the human brain’s most enigmatic hubs. Serving as the primary meeting point where raw physiological signals from the body converge with emotion and conscious thought, the insula shapes everything from acute physical pain and temperature sensation to visceral anxiety and self-awareness.

Yet because of its deep anatomical location, mapping precisely where these distinct functions reside—and how they communicate—has long remained a major challenge in human neuroscience.

In a recent development, now, in a landmark study titled “Functional architecture of the human insula,” an international team led by Dr. Julian Quabs and Professor Dr. Dr. Svenja Caspers at Heinrich Heine University Düsseldorf (HHU) and Forschungszentrum Jülich (FZJ), working alongside collaborators at Stanford University and the National Research Council (CNR) in Parma, has created the first comprehensive functional atlas of the human insula.

To peer directly into the living human insula, the team analyzed intracranial electrophysiological data collected over roughly 15 years at Stanford University Medical Center from 87 patients undergoing diagnostic monitoring for drug-resistant epilepsy.

With patient consent, temporarily implanted depth electrodes allowed investigators to deliver targeted electrical stimulation across the insula while recording real-time sensations, neural activity, and directional connectivity with surrounding cortical networks.

This rare dataset revealed that the human insula is organized into four distinct, cooperating functional zones:.

Crucially, connectivity analyses revealed a powerful directional hierarchy: the cognitive insular pole exerts far stronger downward influence over the sensory rear regions than the sensory zones exert back onto the pole.

According to recent reports, “Our findings show that the insula is more than a relay station for bodily signals. It appears to actively shape how we experience pain and our own bodies,” explained lead author Dr. Julian Quabs, who conducted much of the investigation during a research fellowship at Stanford University.

According to recent reports, “This points to a possible neural mechanism through which emotions and expectations can alter how we perceive pain and other physical sensations,” added senior author Professor Dr. Dr. Svenja Caspers, Director of the Institute of Anatomy I at HHU and head of the Connectivity group at INM-1, FZJ.

By showing how top-down cognitive signals from the frontal lobe and insular pole directly modulate posterior pain-processing regions, the new atlas offers a concrete biological circuit underlying phenomena such as the placebo effect—providing a precise anatomical roadmap for future neuromodulation and chronic pain therapies.

What is the insular cortex (insula), and what does it do?

The insula is a region of cerebral cortex folded deep inside the brain that integrates physical signals from the body—such as pain, temperature, and heartbeat, with emotions and conscious awareness, shaping how we perceive both physical sensations and ourselves.

What are the four functional regions discovered in the new insula atlas?

Researchers divided the human insula into four cooperating zones: an upper rear region with a body-part map for pain and temperature; a lower region for widespread bodily sensations; a middle front region linked to chest/abdominal sensations and anxiety; and the front tip (insular pole), which connects to the frontal lobe to direct attention.

How does this study help explain the placebo effect?

The researchers discovered that the cognitive front tip of the insula (the insular pole) communicates strongly with the frontal lobe and sends powerful top-down signals to the pain-sensing regions at the back of the insula, showing how beliefs, expectations, and emotions can actively dial down physical pain.

Functional architecture of the human insula.

The insular cortex has a central role in pain, interoception and feelings, yet its functional architecture and causal electrophysiological relationships among its subregions remain poorly understood.

Here we combine intracranial electrical stimulation and task-based electroencephalography recordings with connectivity mapping within a cytoarchitectonic atlas of the human insula in 87 participants implanted with intracranial electrodes, and identify a quadripartite functional architecture comprising four distinct regions: (1) a dorsal–posterior region encoding somatotopically organized nociceptive/thermoceptive and somatosensory signals; (2) a ventral–posterior region with access to somatic information across multiple body parts; (3) a mid-anterior region associated with visceral sensations and anxiety states; and (4) an anterior–polar region, largely silent to direct stimulation, yet showing robust activation during salience detection and change of action mode.

Critically, this anterior region, with its strong connections with the prefrontal cortex, including the anterior cingulate cortex, exerts strong and direct influence over other insular regions, while receiving less-strong indirect inputs from them, revealing an electrophysiological pathway for cognitive modulation of pain and bodily perception.

Together, these findings define a functional architecture of the human insula that links cytoarchitecture to directed and asymmetric electrophysiological interactions, with mechanistic implications for cognitive modulation of pain and interoceptive experience.

Blocking Gut Cannabinoid Receptors Restores Memory in Fragile X
