What’s Vital to Us When Making Political Decisions?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1494 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A core assumption in any democracy is that citizens with access to information will make reasoned decisions on political candidates and policy challenges.
  • The paper offers striking insight into the differences in cognitive reasoning patterns among Americans.
  • It has been revealed that “When people make complicated choices with many considerations—which political candidate to support, which immigrant they would rather admit to the country, which climate policy they prefer—we tend to assume they’re weighing all the factors,” mentioned Berkeley political scientist Kirk Bansak.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A core assumption in any democracy is that citizens with access to information will make reasoned decisions on political candidates and policy challenges. But a new study by UC Berkeley social scientists finds that Americans usually don’t consider the full scope of difficult issues, instead basing their opinions on mental shortcuts that sidestep complexity.

The paper offers striking insight into the differences in cognitive reasoning patterns among Americans. While some people in the study did closely analyze a range of complications before coming to an opinion, others did a quick back-of-the-napkin tally of plusses and minuses, or even more commonly based their opinions on just one factor, the authors found.

It has been revealed that “When people make complicated choices with many considerations—which political candidate to support, which immigrant they would rather admit to the country, which climate policy they prefer—we tend to assume they’re weighing all the factors,” mentioned Berkeley political scientist Kirk Bansak. But, he added, “we find that most of them aren’t. Most commonly, people rely on a mental shortcut, effectively deciding based on the single factor they care about most and largely ignoring the rest.”.

For example, when asked to choose between two fictional U.S. Senate candidates based on age, gender, race, education, military experience, and political experience, many of the study participants would make their decision based on just one of those factors.

That doesn’t mean that people are irrational, remarked coauthor Nidhi Banavar, a Berkeley cognitive scientist. “The kind of rationality that we define in the paper is quite different from what many humans actually do in real life,” she explained. “We have these amazing brains, but they’re not the infinite computational machines that would be necessary in order to do the kind of ‘rational’ we imagine in our paper.”.

Still, the findings have clear implications for politics and political communication. For example, Banavar said, if a leader knows that public opinion on climate change is dominated by pocketbook concerns to the exclusion of other problems, then that single factor might weigh heavily in political advertising. Complex science issues, meanwhile, might be downplayed.

It has been revealed that the paper, “Classifying Strategy Use in Multi-Attribute Subjective Choice: Application to Conjoint Experiments in Political Science,” was published recently in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Bansak is an associate professor of political science at UC Berkeley; Banavar is a postdoctoral researcher in political science at UC Berkeley.

Industry observers note that the foundational ideals of American democracy grew from the Enlightenment era some three centuries ago. Central to that framework was a belief that humans, being rational, are capable of governing themselves—and justified in demanding political power. A core concept has been the marketplace of ideas, a constant competition between political and policy goals, looks, and analysis that would inform citizens and help them to govern themselves.

Recent findings suggest that while many eras in U.S. history feature episodes in which reason faltered, modern social scientists have detailed the ways in which cognitive bias, rational ignorance, and other behaviors short-circuit reasoning. Still, the hopeful assumption about human reasoning persists.

Recent findings suggest that social scientists have long studied human decision making at the aggregate level. Banavar and Bansak set out to build a new kind of cognitive model, a complex tool that can enable researchers to see an individual’s decision making mid-process, in detail.

The model doesn’t give them a view into the minds of their research subjects, but the researchers can study hundreds or thousands of decisions by an individual; from these patterns, they can perceive the values and reasoning processes that shape their decisions.

In all, nearly 3,800 people were involved in the study. Each participant sat at a computer screen, and the computer generated a random set of choices in three areas: which migrants they would rather admit to the United States, which Senate primary candidate they would rather vote for, and which climate policy package they would prefer the United States to adopt.

It has been revealed that consider the basic question comparing two hypothetical migrants to the U.S. Their profiles appeared side by side, each described by six factors: region of origin, education level, gender, age, English proficiency, and whether they were seeking economic opportunity or asylum. The research subject would have to choose which of the migrants they preferred to admit to the U.S.

It has been revealed that the computer randomly presented 30 different sets of hypothetical migrants. If a participant consistently chose the younger migrant or the migrant with greater English skills, for example, the researchers could conclude that that was the most important factor for that participant.

The same decision framework was presented for comparing potential climate change policies and fictional U.S. Senate candidates.

The research did yield some insights about basic priorities: Participants preferred younger political candidates. They preferred climate change policy that minimized economic impact on their household. They preferred immigrants who were seeking asylum as opposed to seeking economic opportunity, and those who were below retirement age.

Sources indicate that but that wasn’t the primary purpose of the study. Banavar and Bansak were less interested in what participants decided, and more interested in how they decided.

The results were striking: In 68% of the cases, study participants used shortcuts and did not deeply assess all six factors when choosing between hypothetical Senate candidates, migrants, or climate policies.

Nearly 54% showed a pattern of making choices dominated by one of the six factors. Another 14% took a different shortcut: Given six factors for each candidate or policy, they counted the total number of factors that they preferred for each, then chose the one containing the greater number.

How many used a comprehensive evaluation of all six factors—a rational assessment, without any shortcuts? Just under 30%.

In a recent development, interestingly, Banavar remarked, a majority of participants did not consistently stay with the same strategy. Some might rely on just one factor in choosing a climate policy, while more fully weighing all the factors in deciding which migrant to admit.

“You can’t put people into buckets to say, ‘OK, this is someone who’s actually only going to care about only one thing,’” she said. “People are actually relating differently to each of these different domains and choosing to use different levels of effort, for want of a better term.”.

To understand why people shift strategies will require further research, she said.

In a recent development, the study comes with some important caveats: If a participant favored female candidates, for example, or migrants who were seeking political asylum, and if both choices had those attributes, the participants had to consider other factors. That reduced, but did not eliminate, the pattern of making a choice based on one factor.

But when the researchers asked the participants to rate each profile before choosing one of them, the participants were more inclined to consider all factors in making their choices.

It has been revealed that further, the researchers allowed for only two attributes in their comparisons—male or female, for example, white or Black, or aged in their 50s or 70s. That’s not ideal, Banavar said, but to include multiple races, for example, is too complex for the cognitive model, and would dilute the patterns in the data. In the choice of Senate candidates, the study did not include the fictional candidates’ political parties. That question could provoke such strong, reflexive reactions that it would cloud the findings, she said.

Sources indicate that the authors say their research has crucial implications not just for cognitive research, but for real-world, on-the-ground U.S. political processes.

Industry observers note that often, Bansak remarked, our understanding of public opinion is based on surveys that ask people to choose between complex options defined by many factors. The fresh research reveals analysts that individuals often base their opinions on a single factor, and that can create a clearer picture of what people want in public policy, and why they want it.

“This bears directly on how we interpret the kind of public-opinion and preference data that routinely informs policy debates and news coverage,” he said.

And that understanding, Banavar mentioned, can shape the policy process—and political communication. If leaders present problems in layers of complexity, “how much are people going to read or listen to that?” she asked. “What is the thing that’s really notable to them, given a particular matter? That’s completely lost when you don’t think about the decision-making process.”.

#57599. Latest Update: Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal

Latest Update: Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal

📅 30 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1538 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for people living with chronic back pain, even a simple movement can trigger a sudden surge of pain.
  • Researchers at UC San Diego School of Medicine found that movement-triggered pain in people with chronic low back pain (cLBP) activates a brain network that normally becomes less active during ordinary pain.
  • According to the World Health Organization, low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for people living with chronic back pain, even a simple movement can trigger a sudden surge of pain. Now, scientists have discovered that these painful episodes activate a surprising part of the brain, one closely connected to our sense of identity and how we think about ourselves.

Researchers at UC San Diego School of Medicine found that movement-triggered pain in people with chronic low back pain (cLBP) activates a brain network that normally becomes less active during ordinary pain. The discovery suggests that persistent back pain may become deeply intertwined with a person's sense of self, potentially helping explain why conventional pain treatments often provide limited relief.

According to the World Health Organization, low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide. When pain persists for more than 12 weeks, it is considered chronic. For many patients, everyday movements can provoke sudden flare-ups that make an already difficult condition even harder to manage.

Although the brain plays a central role in how pain is experienced, researchers have struggled to identify the precise brain circuits responsible for pain triggered by movement.

Chronic Back Pain Activates the Brain's Sense of Self.

The new study, published on October 5, 2026, in the British Journal of Anaesthesia, identified an unexpected response involving the brain's Default Mode Network (DMN).

Sources indicate that sometimes called the "self network," the DMN consists of interconnected regions in the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. These areas are especially active when our attention turns inward, such as when we reflect on personal experiences, think about our identity, or consider our thoughts and emotions. In contrast, the network generally becomes less active when we direct our attention toward something happening around us.

The researchers discovered that sudden back pain caused by movement switched this network on rather than off. This unusual response suggests that chronic pain involves more than the processing of physical sensations. It may also engage the brain systems that shape how people experience themselves.

Industry observers note that the findings could help researchers understand why treatments that focus primarily on suppressing pain symptoms do not always work well for chronic low back pain. They also raise the possibility that targeting the DMN could offer a different approach to treatment.

Brain Scans Reveal a Surprising Difference Between Chronic and Acute Pain.

To investigate what happens in the brain during a pain flare, the researchers recruited 114 patients with chronic low back pain.

Each participant completed a "leg raise test," a standard clinical procedure used to provoke back pain. During the test, researchers monitored changes in brain blood flow using a specialized functional MRI method called arterial spin labeling. This technique allows scientists to track patterns of brain activity by measuring blood flow without relying on an injected contrast agent.

According to recent reports, the team also examined how participants responded to a separate painful stimulus. They applied a harmless but uncomfortable heat sensation to the calf, similar to the brief pain someone might experience when accidentally touching a hot stove.

Comparing these two situations revealed a striking difference.

When movement triggered a flare of chronic back pain, the DMN became more active. However, when participants experienced the painful heat stimulus, the same network became less active, following the brain's typical response to acute pain.

The researchers also identified several other important patterns:.

Together, these findings provide new evidence that chronic pain flares involve brain processes associated with personal identity, not just the physical experience of pain.

Why the Brain Reacts Differently to Chronic Pain.

In a recent development, during ordinary acute pain, the brain generally reduces activity in the DMN so it can concentrate on the immediate source of danger. This response helps shift attention away from internal thoughts and toward an external threat.

But the UC San Diego researchers found that movement triggered chronic back pain produced the opposite effect.

Sources indicate that "In every pain study, when you're experiencing pain, the DMN deactivates," remarked corresponding author Fadel Zeidan, PhD, professor in the Department of Anesthesiology, endowed professor at the Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion, and director of the Pain Health and Mindfulness Laboratory at UC San Diego School of Medicine. "What we show for the first time ever is that when you have a pain flare, it turns on instead. You start to identify the experience with who you are.".

Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest that chronic back pain can become closely connected with the brain's internal representation of the self. Rather than processing pain solely as a physical warning signal, the brain may also link it to personal memories, expectations, and emotional experiences.

It has been revealed that for someone living with chronic pain, this means the experience can extend far beyond the moments when the pain is physically present. Worry about the next flare, memories of previous episodes, and fear of movements that might trigger pain can all become part of everyday life.

"The moment-to-moment experience is contaminated not only by the feeling of pain, but by the anticipation of it and recovery from it. It's contaminated by past experiences like embarrassment about not being able to participate in normal activities and fear of movement when trying to avoid the pain.".

This connection between pain and personal identity may help explain why chronic back pain can be especially difficult to treat.

A New Direction for Chronic Back Pain Treatment.

Because movement-triggered chronic back pain engages different brain networks from ordinary acute pain, researchers believe traditional treatments may fail to address some of the processes that sustain the experience of chronic pain.

Medications such as opiates primarily target pain signaling, but they may not adequately address the brain networks involved in the emotional and personal dimensions of persistent pain.

Sources indicate that "Current pain medicine is fixated on ridding patients of their pain symptoms, but that's not the source of chronic pain. These data suggest that a chronic pain flare also encompasses one's identity.".

The discovery points toward treatments that address not only the sensation of pain but also the brain's relationship with that sensation.

Recent work by Zeidan and his colleagues has explored two potential approaches: mindfulness meditation and the psychedelic compound psilocybin.

Both approaches are being investigated for their ability to help people experience physical pain without allowing it to become as closely tied to their identity. Early findings suggest that changing this relationship may reduce pain intensity, although additional research is needed to confirm the results and determine how effective these treatments may be.

In a recent development, "These types of mind-body and psychedelic medicine approaches target the whole person," Zeidan remarked. "Mindfulness is a meditation technique that's about cultivating non-judgmental awareness of the present moment that dramatically reduces pain in a very unique way. Psilocybin seemingly resets the pain system that integrates trauma, past experiences and future worries to facilitate a restart, if you will. They're not a silver bullet -- you're not necessarily getting rid of the pain, but you're changing the relationship you have with that pain so it doesn't contaminate your everyday life.".

Can Mindfulness and Psychedelics Change How the Brain Experiences Pain?

Rather than attempting to eliminate every pain signal, these approaches aim to change how the brain interprets and responds to the experience.

Recent findings suggest that mindfulness meditation encourages people to observe their thoughts, emotions, and physical sensations without immediately judging or reacting to them. Psilocybin, meanwhile, is being studied for its potential to alter brain processes that connect pain with earlier experiences, emotional distress, and expectations about the future.

The goal is not necessarily to remove pain altogether, but to reduce how much it influences a person's thoughts, emotions, and daily functioning.

According to recent reports, zeidan's laboratory is at the moment conducting several clinical trials using brain imaging to investigate whether mindfulness meditation and psychedelic treatments can change the neural processes involved in self-reflection. Researchers hope to determine whether these approaches can reshape brain activity and improve how people subjectively experience chronic pain.

In a recent development, although the research remains at an early stage, the findings offer a different way to think about persistent back pain. Understanding why the brain connects chronic pain with a person's sense of self could eventually help scientists develop treatments that address aspects of pain that conventional therapies often miss.

Additional study authors from UC San Diego School of Medicine include Morgan Gianola, Jon Dean, Conan Chen, Daniel Barrows, Gabriel Reigner, and Thomas Liu.

#57598. Can You Learn to Feel More Loved?

Can You Learn to Feel More Loved?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine you have a colleague who remembers that you had a difficult appointment and checks in on you.
  • Sources indicate that in our research, we coined the term felt love to focus on the receiver’s side of love.
  • In a recent development, in our research on shared beliefs about love, we asked 495 people representative of the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine you have a colleague who remembers that you had a difficult appointment and checks in on you. Or a friend who is just there to listen without telling you what you should have done differently. We don’t tend to think of these experiences as grand declarations of love, but they leave us with a certain lingering warmth: the feeling of being loved.

Sources indicate that in our research, we coined the term felt love to focus on the receiver’s side of love. This emphasis shifts attention away from the expressions of love (i.e., loving signals). While expressions are actions we choose to take, felt love is an internal, subjective sensation that washes over us. However, how strongly it does so also depends on us: The same act of care may pass unnoticed or land as love, based on the receiver’s cognitive beliefs or state of mind. Many experiences may elicit felt love, and they occur not only in romantic settings, but when we share time with friends, receive supportive gestures from family, or even get unexpected help from strangers. We are only just beginning to uncover how people come to feel loved and whether that experience can be changed—if it can be learned, like a skill.

In a recent development, in our research on shared beliefs about love, we asked 495 people representative of the U.S. population to judge situations that would make most people feel loved. What they ranked most love-eliciting was being shown compassion in difficult times—an act that, in principle, any person could (and should) offer. Pets feeling happy to see them ranked highly for eliciting the feeling of being loved. Clearly, love, as people live it day to day, reaches past courtship and partnership.

It has been revealed that work like this partly drives how we measure who feels loved and when. It is common for studies to measure the experience of love as if it were a stable trait—for example, romantic attachment as a demographic indicator—but this practice obscures fundamental aspects of the lived human story. Relationship status may describe part of someone’s circumstances, but it does not tell us whether that person feels loved in their daily experience. For example, many people experience love while unattached, and many do not experience love despite being in a long-term relationship. In fact, in our studies, strong experiences of felt love are reported by participants who identify as unattached. To study felt love, we also have to ask about the experience directly.

Subjective states like felt love are inherently volatile, so studying it requires many careful observations, ideally while people are going about their daily lives. We often rely on complex research methods that focus not only on how people feel at a given time, but on the patterns of change over time and how those are shaped by our environment and affected by others. Our basic approach is simple in principle: Ask people how loved they feel at different times while they go about their lives. In two studies published in 2020, in which over 200 participants reported their felt love states a handful of times per day for several weeks, we found that people with higher levels of felt love also tended to report greater flourishing and emotional well-being.

Frequent, repeated observations also allow us to disentangle a person’s typical experience from day-to-day fluctuations. This can also reveal individual differences in how persistent daily felt love states are—a feeling can be strong and brief, or weaker but sustained. Persistence is not automatically desirable: A below-usual feeling of being loved can persist, too. Whether particular patterns directly affect well-being remains an key open question.

To study the role of persistence, we developed custom mathematical models that include love inertia—that is, how long that warm feeling stays with us. In our recently published study, 52 participants reported how loved they felt as well as how much love they had expressed over a period of 28 days. We found that people whose felt love states were more persistent also enjoyed better mental health and indicators of well-being. Even more interestingly, the more people expressed love to others in their daily lives, the more they themselves tended to feel loved in return. Expressing love appears to be a gift that keeps on giving: Showing love is associated with a lasting sense of warmth and better well-being, and it also spreads love around you.

It has been revealed that this finding suggests an actionable insight: Expressing love could be one route to feeling loved. If you are feeling a lack of connection, proactively expressing selfless care for someone else might help jumpstart your own feelings of being loved. We don’t yet know what accounts for this association. Expressing love might invite a warm response, change how you interpret a relationship, or be part of an interaction that lifts both people up.

Industry observers note that can an interaction actually change how loved someone feels? A 2024 study with 218 parent–child pairs argues just that. The authors of that study randomly assigned parents and their children, aged eight to 13, to one of two nine-minute conversations. In one condition, they took turns answering questions that encouraged personal disclosure (for example, instead of a surface-level question like “How was school?,” they might ask, “What is something you worry about?”). In the other condition, they made small talk. Children in the disclosure condition reported feeling more loved during the conversation.

Recent findings suggest that this result cannot readily be explained by children in warmer families simply choosing more personal conversations—assignment of children to conditions was random. The researchers changed the conversation and observed a direct difference in the children’s experience.

In a recent development, such findings need to be independently replicated for reliability and generalizability, but this is an important and promising step: A straightforward intervention changed an experience of feeling loved. The next question we can work on is whether changes of this kind can become part of daily life.

This piece is part of a three-year GGSC project to explore love's role in promoting social well-being, bridging divides, and contributing to a good, meaningful life.

Our focus on the receiver side of love brings a slightly more complex perspective: that an act does not produce a loving feeling by itself, but that effect is moderated by interpretation and expectation—thoughts that come to us in the moment, cognitive beliefs that support those thoughts, and the justifications we have for those beliefs. A colleague’s quiet help can be experienced as love, or dismissed as routine professional courtesy.

Sources indicate that an area that is not yet well-explored is how the reception of expressions of love can be taught. If feelings follow perceptions, and perceptions follow beliefs, then felt love is a cognitive phenomenon in addition to an emotional one, so that cognitive skills contribute to how we experience the social world. It may be possible for people to learn to notice when they reflexively dismiss acts of care, to check their interpretation against what actually happened, and to re-evaluate in order to let the sender’s kindness count. It is also possible that a deficit in this cognitive skill prohibits many people from benefiting from the ambient love that is already present in everyday life. Even so, biased perceptions can have positive effects in this context. People with a stronger general tendency to interpret daily life experiences as expressions of love feel more loved in general, with all the well-being benefits that brings.

According to recent reports, we now have ways to measure felt love in daily life, evidence linking it to well-being, and at least one experiment that changed it in the moment. A sensible next step is to connect those findings.

Can an intervention change daily feelings of love for weeks or months? Does that change lead to better well-being? Does it work for people who start out feeling relatively unloved, or mainly for those already doing well? Those are different questions, all embedded in the vastly complex network of our daily environments and experiences—part of what is sometimes called the exposome—and they require different, carefully drawn comparisons.

Future trials could focus on the cognitive component of felt love—whether an underlying ability to appreciate acts of love extends to other facets of life, and whether interventions should target the individual’s reasoning before focusing on their social context. Repeated measurements in daily-life settings could be used to show whether any differences generated by the intervention survive after the study session. Such trials would need to be designed with a great deal of care to establish the mechanisms of causality—a standard challenge of daily-life social psychology studies, but an especially critical one here. Establishing how to make experiences of felt love more available is an expansive but worthwhile scientific endeavor.

Finally, an emerging focus on love also recognizes how it is culturally and contextually bound. While certain loving gestures are found all over the world (such as helping someone in need, or empathic attention), to foster intercultural understanding, empathy, and inclusivity in diverse societies, it is vital to recognize love’s cultural variations in everyday life. We are right now conducting global cross-cultural research to identify specific ways love is shown in everyday life across different types of relationships, beyond just the romantic.

While we and other researchers continue to conduct larger studies to unpack these exact mechanisms, we don’t have to wait for the data to start paying closer attention to the quiet moments in our own lives. What happens when you feel genuinely cared for? What happens when you proactively express love to someone else? Being mindful of how they respond can reveal something that checking a box to count affectionate gestures misses. Fostering these experiences doesn’t require a laboratory—it is a daily practice we can all begin right now. Showing love is a low-cost experiment we can all conduct in our own daily lives.

Zita Oravecz, Ph.D., is a professor of human development and family studies at Penn State and a faculty co-hire in the Institute for Computational and Data Sciences. An expert in quantitative psychology, she develops Bayesian and dynamic statistical models that show how shared beliefs and individual feelings change over time.

Scientists discover a surprising brain benefit of eating peanuts every day

📅 01 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, eating peanuts every day may offer surprising benefits for the aging brain.
  • Although insulin is best known for regulating blood sugar, it also plays an essential role in the brain.
  • After participants consumed peanuts daily for 16 weeks, researchers observed improved insulin responsiveness in a group of brain regions in the right hemisphere.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, eating peanuts every day may offer surprising benefits for the aging brain. Researchers at Maastricht University Medical Center in the Netherlands have found that regularly consuming unsalted, skin-roasted peanuts can improve how certain brain regions respond to insulin in older adults. The findings come from the Institute of Nutrition and Translational Research in Metabolism (NUTRIM) and were published in the peer-reviewed journal Food & Function.

Although insulin is best known for regulating blood sugar, it also plays an essential role in the brain. It helps nerve cells grow, survive, and communicate with one another, supporting memory and other cognitive abilities. Healthy insulin signaling may also help protect against processes associated with Alzheimer's disease.

After participants consumed peanuts daily for 16 weeks, researchers observed improved insulin responsiveness in a group of brain regions in the right hemisphere. These included portions of the lingual gyrus, hippocampus, parahippocampal gyrus, and posterior cingulate gyrus, all of which contribute to memory-related processes.

"The hormone insulin plays an key role in the brain, where it supports memory and other cognitive processes. As people age, the brain may become less responsive to insulin, which has been linked to age-related cognitive decline," says Dr. Peter Joris, the study's senior author and an associate professor in the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences, NUTRIM, Maastricht University Medical Center. "Our study found that daily peanut consumption beneficially affected insulin responsiveness in memory-related brain regions in older adults. These findings suggest that enhanced regional brain insulin responsiveness may contribute to the cognitive benefits of unsalted, skin-roasted peanut intake.".

Daily Peanuts Linked to Better Memory and Brain Blood Flow.

According to recent reports, the study included 31 healthy adults between the ages of 60 and 75. During the peanut consumption phase, participants ate 60 grams (approximately two servings) of peanuts each day for 16 weeks. Researchers used a randomized, controlled crossover trial, a rigorous study design that allowed them to compare the effects of eating peanuts with those of avoiding them.

Industry observers note that the new findings build on earlier research by Joris published in 2025. That investigation found that consuming peanuts for 16 weeks increased overall cerebral blood flow (CBF) by 3.6% and improved verbal memory performance by 5.8%.

Cerebral blood flow measures how much blood circulates through the brain, carrying oxygen and nutrients that brain cells need to function properly. It is an crucial indicator of the health of the brain's blood vessels. Those earlier results appeared in the peer-reviewed journal Clinical Nutrition.

How Scientists Measured the Effects of Peanuts on the Brain.

One distinguishing feature of the NUTRIM research was its combination of a carefully controlled dietary intervention lasting several months with sophisticated brain imaging technology.

To examine changes in brain function, researchers used arterial spin labeling magnetic resonance imaging (ASL-MRI), a technique that measures blood flow in different regions of the brain. They evaluated insulin responsiveness by tracking changes in regional cerebral blood flow after insulin was administered through the nose.

In a recent development, the team also used abdominal MRI scans to measure fat accumulation in the liver, known as intrahepatic lipid (IHL) content. Cognitive abilities were assessed using the Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB), a standardized collection of computerized tests.

Researchers believe several components of peanuts may contribute to their observed effects on brain health, rather than any single nutrient being responsible.

It has been revealed that "Multiple nutrients present in peanuts, including unsaturated fats, dietary fiber, vitamins and minerals and bioactive phytochemicals, could potentially contribute to the observed brain benefits," says Joris. "Peanuts are also a good source of plant-based protein and are especially rich in L-arginine. L-arginine is a key precursor of nitric oxide (NO), which has been reported to facilitate learning and memory performance.".

What Participants Ate During the 16-Week Study.

To ensure participants consumed a consistent amount, researchers supplied premeasured packets of skin-roasted peanuts throughout the peanut intervention period.

Participants were instructed to eat their peanuts in the morning or afternoon, but they could choose how to incorporate them into their daily routine. They could consume the entire portion at once, divide it into smaller amounts throughout the day, or include the peanuts in their meals.

It has been revealed that during the control phase, participants avoided peanuts entirely. After 16 weeks, they switched to the opposite study condition, allowing researchers to compare brain health measurements under both dietary approaches.

According to recent reports, the study was led by principal investigator Associate Professor Dr. Peter J. Joris and conducted by Ph.D. candidate Lucia Kerkhof of the Department of Nutrition and Movement Sciences at Maastricht University Medical Center.

In a recent development, funding was provided by The Peanut Institute Foundation. According to the researchers, the foundation had no involvement in designing or conducting the study, analyzing or interpreting the results, or preparing the manuscript.

How Young People Are Researching Issues That Matter to Them

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2172 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Adults should take students more seriously, as they have voices and different opinions too” — Middle school student.
  • Industry observers note that middle school students in a California school district noticed that their perspectives were not included in decisions related to school policy that they cared about, like the dress code.
  • According to recent reports, many youth across the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Adults should take students more seriously, as they have voices and different opinions too” — Middle school student.

Industry observers note that middle school students in a California school district noticed that their perspectives were not included in decisions related to school policy that they cared about, like the dress code. They engaged in research to explore how administrators, teachers, and staff could incorporate their voices in decision-making processes. Students conducted surveys and focus groups with their peers and developed recommendations for their school, including more student-led events and a more active role engaged in school policy discussions. The following semester, the principal added students to several school leadership committees, where they helped inform programs and policies beyond the dress code, such as student social events and classroom curricular activities.

According to recent reports, many youth across the U.S. report feeling disengaged and disconnected from their schools, which is associated with declining attendance and greater mental health challenges. Addressing these challenges is critical, especially because a sense of belonging and connectedness predicts attendance, academic success, social well-being, self-esteem, and other positive outcomes for students.

Research is one key way to seek out solutions to these problems, and Youth Participatory Action Research (YPAR) is an innovative and growing approach that engages youth as experts to improve their lives, communities, and youth-serving institutions. In middle and high schools across the U.S., students in YPAR classes conduct research to inform policies, practices, and peer education efforts. They have prioritized and addressed a wide range of academic and school-climate concerns, such as improving teacher-student relationships, peer relationships, safety, and school lunch options; and reducing disproportionate discipline, substance use, and transit barriers.

Sources indicate that in schools that provide opportunities for YPAR, students are trained to take up roles as researchers, knowledge producers, and changemakers who contribute to their school communities. Further, YPAR evidence can deepen adults’ understanding of what shapes students’ feelings of belonging, patterns of engagement, and well-being. YPAR findings thus can inform more relevant and responsive solutions that can benefit youth, adults, and the broader community. This article provides guidance for educators who work with K–12 students and are interested in implementing YPAR.

Here are three examples of how YPAR impacts different levels of the school “ecosystem.”.

Systems-level: High school YPAR students in an Ohio school district explored whether their school provided adequate mental health services. They conducted a schoolwide survey, and their findings revealed that although there were mental health services available, many students were not aware of them. In response, the student researchers took action and developed more promotional materials and held informational assemblies to raise awareness of these services. They also held meetings with teachers, counselors, administrators, and the superintendent to discuss potential districtwide solutions to improve mental health services and access.

It has been revealed that relationships: Middle school YPAR students in a California school district identified that they didn’t feel supported by their teachers. To explore this problem further, they conducted surveys and focus groups with their peers on teacher-student relationships. Their findings offered concrete suggestions on how teachers could improve their mentorship relationships with students, including practicing active listening, showing respect and compassion, being more flexible with assignments, and incorporating more engaging classroom activities that lift up student voices. The students also recommended student-led teacher evaluations.

Student-level: High school YPAR students in a California school district conducted English and Spanish focus groups with their peers on attendance and belonging. Based on their findings, the YPAR students proposed buddy programs to connect newly introduced students with their peers, schoolwide workshops to raise awareness on racial stereotyping, and lunchtime soccer tournaments to increase a sense of belonging.

Read more stories on our YPAR Hub.

It has been revealed that our YPAR Design Guide offers several considerations when deciding whether YPAR is a fit for your program or setting. YPAR has been primarily implemented with middle and high school students, and is well-suited to strengthening the developmental capacities of youth in early, middle, and late adolescence. However, elementary school students have also engaged in successful YPAR projects using mapping and arts-based methods.

First, adult facilitators (for example, teachers or program leaders) should assess capacity and consider whether there are adequate resources to pursue the YPAR project, including the timeframe of the project, staffing required, whether funding is needed, and the setting and scope.

Second, adult facilitators can introduce YPAR to students in a way that meets them “where they are at.” Not every student will be interested in YPAR from the start. Some may have had limited exposure to research, and others may not have had positive experiences (for example, through a particularly challenging or frustrating class assignment). Facilitators can engage the students in activities that lift up their experiences, then generate excitement by framing research as a tool for exploring and taking action on the issues that students care about.

Explore compassion, self-compassion, and awe with educators around the world.

Industry observers note that facilitators should also work with students to clarify their motivations for the project: What is the purpose of the project? What do students hope to get out of participating in YPAR? And what does their desired impact look like? In several projects, we have seen students become more interested in YPAR as they move through the process, analyze data, and develop their action looks and recommendations.

In a recent development, finally, adult facilitators should be attentive to the broader context surrounding the topic or glitch. For example, if the research is on safety and well-being, what programs or initiatives are already focusing on these problems, both in and out of school (for example, community health organizations)? What are the relevant constraints (for example, barriers accessing decision-making processes)? And where might there be opportunities to partner and collaborate? Understanding these factors will help adult facilitators and students choose an area of focus that aligns with their goals.

YPAR is not “one size fits all.” Adult YPAR facilitators adapt YPAR across a multitude of settings, including schools, afterschool programs, and community-based organizations such as youth centers. Even within schools, a YPAR process can vary in length. For example, some YPAR projects span a single unit within a semester; others may take up an entire semester, and in some cases extend across a full academic year (fall and spring semesters).

According to recent reports, further, YPAR is sometimes conducted as part of a club or extracurricular activity outside of formal class time. While the structure and duration of YPAR projects vary, many projects follow these steps: building the team, identifying and defining an matter or problem, selecting a research design and methods, collecting data, analyzing and interpreting results, developing action plans and recommendations, disseminating findings, and taking action.

Throughout the YPAR process, young people serve as leaders who decide on the topic, matter, and questions they wish to investigate. Adult facilitators serve as supportive guides and mentors, training them in research methods focused on generating numerical data or text- and image-based data. Youth then go on to collect and analyze their data and develop actions plans and recommendations to address their selected problem.

According to recent reports, A core value in YPAR is authentic power-sharing between adult facilitators and youth researchers. Most of the time, youth navigate learning spaces where they are “receivers” of knowledge from adults. Further, in traditional adult-led research projects, youth typically serve only as “respondents” to surveys or interviews, with no say in the research questions, methods, or interpretation.

You can learn more about YPAR practice and research by accessing the following resources: YPAR Hub: One-stop shop for YPAR lesson plans and other resources YPAR Network: A broad network of diverse YPAR scholars and practitioners that will expand and refine YPAR practice, and increase the reach, evidence base, and impact of YPAR. Locate our YPAR online training modules here. IRB resources for researchers who want to study YPAR and a supplemental article.

YPAR Hub: One-stop shop for YPAR lesson looks and other resources.

YPAR Network: A broad network of diverse YPAR scholars and practitioners that will expand and refine YPAR practice, and increase the reach, evidence base, and impact of YPAR. Locate our YPAR online training modules here.

IRB resources for researchers who want to study YPAR and a supplemental article.

It has been revealed that the YPAR approach challenges these dynamics by positioning youth as knowledge generators who combine lived-experience expertise with systematic data-based inquiry. Youth researchers have decision-making power and are primary drivers of the YPAR process, while adults serve as guides to help them in advancing their projects.

It has been revealed that power-sharing is a learnable and teachable set of skills. Our guide provides lessons and activities that help facilitators attend to power dynamics, along with strategies that support power-sharing throughout YPAR. Adults and youth can productively share power in research when supportive structures are in place.

The results from YPAR research may (or may not) result in policy or practice change. Adult facilitators play a critical role in strategically connecting YPAR evidence to key decision-making spaces and helping implement youth action looks.

One step that facilitators can take is identifying existing decision-making structures where there may be opportunities to integrate YPAR evidence. They can also determine whether new routines need to be established. High School youth in Colorado investigated practices (through student surveys) that they noticed enhanced student-teacher relationships. Students then developed and led a day-long professional development for teachers on how small adjustments to the start of the year, including taking time to build trust and rapport before reviewing the syllabi, could increase student engagement and buy-in.

Industry observers note that in our work, students have consistently emphasized how much it matters for adults to “keep them in the loop,” reporting back on whether and how their YPAR evidence was used. Authentically integrating YPAR evidence involves being transparent with students and following up with them throughout the process. Adults should take YPAR evidence seriously and actively prevent tokenizing processes—in other words, where YPAR evidence becomes a check-the-box rather than meaningful engagement. Ultimately, adults supporting YPAR must take an active role in creating conditions where youth feel safe, heard, and valued.

In a recent development, there is growing interest in YPAR at the local, state, and national levels, and it aligns with many initiatives that are already happening in schools. For example, the National Institutes of Health identified YPAR as a promising approach to address conditions that affect mental health and well-being, such as social isolation and exposure to unsafe environments. In California, SB997 mandates student voice be integrated in school and district budgeting processes. Oregon, Ohio, and Newly introduced Jersey have similar mandates that require youth voice in decision making. There are strong synergies between YPAR and social-emotional learning programs, which are implemented in many school sites. YPAR also aligns with many academic competencies and standards, offering students a unique opportunity to build durable academic and career skills.

Recent findings suggest that students care about their schools and want to improve them. Adults need to learn along with them, listen to them, value their ideas, and support them in making change.

Breaking: Four Practices to Help You Feel More Engaged at Work

💡 Key Takeaways
  • With only 20% of workers feeling engaged globally, we need tools that can help boost engagement and well-being at work.
  • While some difficulty at work may always be expected, there are things we can do to take control of our work lives and bring more kindness, appreciation, connection, and trust into the workplace.
  • Industry observers note that you can find some of these on Greater Good in Action, our library of over 100 practices found to improve well-being.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Work can be tough. With only 20% of workers feeling engaged globally, we need tools that can help boost engagement and well-being at work.

While some difficulty at work may always be expected, there are things we can do to take control of our work lives and bring more kindness, appreciation, connection, and trust into the workplace. For many years, researchers have been testing different practices that individual employees, managers, and teams can do to improve work life for everyone.

Industry observers note that you can find some of these on Greater Good in Action, our library of over 100 practices found to improve well-being. Each practice includes:.

Recently, we added four new practices that you might want to try in your workplace.

Industry observers note that let’s face it: We don’t always feel appreciated at work, even though appreciation seems to be a key need for most people. In this practice, you begin a regular team meeting with the simple act of appreciating the person to your left. You say something specific about one of their qualities or an action they took and the impact it had on you. Then that person appreciates the person to their left, and you go around the room (or virtual meeting) until everyone gets appreciated.

Sources indicate that years ago, I tested this practice in a meeting with a team I was working with. When we got to the third person being appreciated, she broke down into tears. She said, “I’ve been working here for nine years, and I didn’t know you guys appreciate me. . . . I didn’t even know you liked me.”.

Help everyone on your team feel appreciated to boost connection and performance.

While this was hard to hear, it’s also a problem that is pretty easy to fix. Appreciation Circles, which can be repeated regularly, try to establish a culture and ritual of appreciation so that no one has to feel undervalued at work.

This practice is designed for managers during their regular (and sometimes less than inspiring) one-on-one meetings with their direct reports. It recommends that you ask employees these three questions:.

According to recent reports, as managers, sometimes we don’t realize the impact of our time with employees. Research suggests that our supportive behaviors can go a long way to helping employees feel more engaged. So how can managers be more supportive?

Improve employee satisfaction and engagement with a guided conversation.

Industry observers note that one study found that when managers encouraged, assured, and valued employee efforts, employees felt more engaged. These are the themes that the three questions in this practice address.

According to recent reports, the question of how you build trust has always been a fascinating one for me, because trust is so foundational to getting things done and is such an important part of a healthy workplace culture. Studies suggest that high-trust work cultures are often higher-performing, but how do you actually earn trust at work?

In their analysis of hundreds of studies on trust, researchers found that there are three key levers for building trust: demonstrating your ability, benevolence, and integrity. In other words, people trust you more when they believe you can get things done, have their best interests at heart, and follow through on your word.

Demonstrate your trustworthiness to your coworkers.

This practice helps you identify ways to show others that you have these qualities by considering three questions and then acting on your answers:.

This practice is probably one of the more fun and feel-good practices because it encourages you to offer some random acts of kindness to your coworkers and see if this creates a multiplier effect in your workplace.

For example, you could bring a coworker a cup of coffee, help them with a project, or offer a handwritten thank-you note.

Do something nice for coworkers and watch kindness spread.

Studies suggest that kind and helpful behaviors can be contagious to those receiving the kind acts, and that even bystanders see boosts in their well-being just from observing these acts.

We encourage you to try this low-risk and feel-good practice in your workplace soon—as well as the rest of them! Keep in touch and let us know how these practices land in your workplace.

Kia Afcari is the director of Greater Good Workplaces at GGSC. He has over 20 years of experience helping leaders, teams, and organizations with collaborative change and has served as a consultant to a wide variety of organizations, including tech, biotech, and fintech companies, health care organizations, universities, NGOs, UN agencies, and nonprofits.

Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1572 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that you walk out of the grocery store, ready to head home and make dinner.
  • Remembering personal experiences like these depends on episodic memory, which allows us to recall events from our lives.
  • This ability tends to weaken as we grow older.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that you walk out of the grocery store, ready to head home and make dinner. But as you scan the crowded parking lot, a frustrating question comes to mind. Where did you leave your car? You try to picture the spot, but the memory refuses to surface.

Remembering personal experiences like these depends on episodic memory, which allows us to recall events from our lives. These memories help form the foundation of long-term memory, whether they involve a childhood milestone, such as the first day of elementary school, or something that happened just minutes earlier, like parking your car.

This ability tends to weaken as we grow older. The sights, sounds, and other details associated with past experiences can become increasingly difficult to retrieve. Scientists still do not fully understand why this happens. Although some memory decline is a common part of aging, the changes can become far more severe in people developing Alzheimer's disease.

A new study from researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, offers notable clues about what may be happening inside the aging brain. Neuroscientist Omer Sharon and his colleagues, working under the direction of former Berkeley sleep researcher Matthew Walker, discovered a connection between disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, declining memory performance, and the accumulation of tau, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease.

The findings suggest that tau buildup in the brain's frontal cortex is linked to changes in the coordinated electrical activity that helps preserve memories overnight.

"This is the first time we've shown this relationship between tau and how it messes with memory consolidation by attenuating traveling slow waves that originate in the frontal cortex," noted Sharon, a postdoctoral researcher at UC Berkeley's Center for Human Sleep Science.

The research was published in Nature Neuroscience.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Store Memories.

Recent findings suggest that sleep involves several distinct stages, each associated with different patterns of brain activity. Rapid eye movement sleep is particularly recognizable because the eyes move beneath closed eyelids and most dreaming takes place during this stage. However, another stage, known as non-REM sleep, is especially key for maintaining healthy brain function.

Recent findings suggest that during this deeper stage of sleep, when dreaming is limited or absent, large groups of neurons briefly become inactive and then active again in a coordinated sequence. These synchronized changes produce slow electrical waves that spread across the brain, typically beginning in the frontal cortex.

"Each slow wave reflects an enormous population of neurons switching off and back on together," Sharon remarked. "Our study demonstrates that for memory, it's critical that these events cascade in sequence across large parts of the brain. This coordinated shutdown has been observed only during deep sleep, and may be one reason why we sleep.".

The researchers found that this carefully organized activity becomes less coordinated as tau accumulates in the aging brain. Instead of traveling together across broad regions, the waves become more scattered and cover shorter distances. These changes are associated with weaker memory consolidation, declining cognitive abilities, and Alzheimer's disease.

Alzheimer's Protein Linked to Disrupted Brain Waves.

To investigate the relationship, the scientists monitored sleeping brain activity using electroencephalograms (EEGs). They compared cognitively healthy young adults in their early 20s with older participants ranging from their mid-60s to mid-70s.

It has been revealed that the differences were striking. In younger participants, groups of slow waves moved together across distances roughly equivalent to the width of a hand on the scalp. Among older adults, the waves typically traveled less far and appeared more independently, rather than moving in coordinated groups.

The team also examined whether these changes were associated with tau accumulation. Working with Dr. William Jagust, a UC Berkeley professor emeritus of public health and neuroscience, the researchers used positron emission tomography (PET) scans to examine the brains of older participants. This imaging technique uses radioactive tracers introduced into the bloodstream to reveal biological activity and the distribution of specific substances.

The scans indicated that greater tau buildup in the frontal cortex was associated with a breakdown in the longer traveling waves normally seen during deep sleep.

Importantly, these changes were present in people who had not developed Alzheimer's disease.

"These people did not have Alzheimer's," Sharon said. "They had tau in their brains, but with subclinical impacts. Their memory decline was within the normal range for their age.".

Sharon explained that early Alzheimer's related changes can vary considerably in severity. The amount of tau present in the brain is associated with cognitive performance, even when a person's memory abilities remain within the expected range for their age.

Mysterious "Lonely Waves" Linked to Memory Loss.

The researchers wanted to determine whether the altered sleep patterns were associated with actual differences in how well people remembered information.

Industry observers note that to test this, participants learned pairs of associated words in the evening. The following day, they were asked to recall what they had learned, allowing the scientists to evaluate how effectively the memories had been retained overnight.

Participants whose slow brain waves traveled shorter distances and appeared more isolated generally remembered fewer word associations. The researchers called these disconnected patterns "lonely waves.".

Recent findings suggest that the team also tracked a subset of participants over several years to see how their brains changed with time. Among those whose frontal cortex tau levels increased, the slow waves became less coordinated, and their ability to retain newly learned information overnight declined.

These observations provide evidence of a relationship between tau accumulation, changes in deep sleep brain activity, and worsening episodic memory. However, they do not establish that tau buildup directly causes memory loss or that disrupted waves are the mechanism responsible.

Additional Tests Strengthen the Connection.

Because PET scans are costly and require specialized facilities, the scientists sought another way to investigate the relationship between Alzheimer's related proteins and sleep activity.

Sources indicate that they collaborated with neurologist Yo-El Ju at Washington University in St. Louis to analyze spinal fluid from a separate group of older adults. The goal was to determine whether measurements of Alzheimer's associated proteins would reveal patterns similar to those seen with brain imaging.

Unlike PET scans, the spinal fluid measurements could not identify tau accumulation specifically within the frontal cortex. Nevertheless, the results pointed in the same direction.

People whose sleeping brains produced more isolated slow waves had higher ratios of tau to amyloid, another protein closely associated with Alzheimer's disease, in their spinal fluid.

The consistency between these independent groups and testing methods strengthened the researchers' confidence in the findings.

"It's collected in a totally different place and in a different cohort, so I think that adds to the strength of the evidence," Sharon said.

Together, the sleep recordings, brain scans, spinal fluid analyses, and memory assessments suggest that tau accumulation is associated with a particular disruption of brain activity during deep sleep.

"This longitudinal correlation suggests that Alzheimer's disease pathology is associated with a disruption of this main sleep feature," Sharon mentioned.

What Deep Sleep Reveals About the Aging Brain.

Recent findings suggest that although memory often declines with age, the newly introduced research indicates that the process may involve more than simply growing older. Changes associated with Alzheimer's disease, particularly tau accumulation in regions responsible for generating widespread slow waves, may help explain why some people experience greater difficulty retaining memories.

Recent findings suggest that "It's not just about age," Sharon said. "It's how much pathology you have in frontal areas where global waves originate.".

Recent findings suggest that sleep quality also appears to be part of the picture. Although it can be difficult to define or measure precisely, the organization and movement of slow brain waves may provide crucial indicators of how effectively the brain performs its nighttime memory functions.

It has been revealed that the findings raise the possibility that changes in deep sleep activity could eventually help researchers better understand or identify early memory problems. They also point toward potential targets for future treatments aimed at protecting memory as people age.

Industry observers note that for now, however, a central question remains unanswered. Scientists still need to determine whether accumulating tau contributes to the breakdown of synchronized sleep waves, whether changes in those waves influence tau accumulation, or whether the relationship involves additional processes.

In a recent development, "We can see tau and lonely waves rising together over time," Sharon stated. "What we cannot yet say is which leads -- and that question will shape how we design interventions.".

The study's additional co-authors include Xi Chen, James Westphal, Chelsea Brown, and Vyoma D. Shah of UC Berkeley, along with Jason Dude of Washington University in St. Louis.

Sources indicate that funding came from grants awarded by the National Institute on Aging at the National Institutes of Health. Sharon also received support through a Glenn Foundation for Medical Research Postdoctoral Fellowship and a Weill Neurohub Fellowship.

How to Start a Side Business While Working Full-Time

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • The number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy.
  • Recent findings suggest that validation does not require a perfect product.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy. Before you spend a dollar on a website, business cards, or inventory, you need to validate that real people will pay real money for what you are offering.

Recent findings suggest that validation does not require a perfect product. It requires proof of demand. Talk to 10 people who match your target customer. Describe what you strategy to offer. Ask two questions: "Would you pay for this?" and "How much would you pay?" If 3 or more say yes with a specific dollar amount, you have a viable idea. If most say "that sounds cool" but hesitate on paying, you have a hobby.

Recent findings suggest that the FI community has a particular advantage here. Many FI seekers have already cut their expenses to the point where a side business does not need to generate massive revenue to make a meaningful impact. Even $500 to $1,000 per month in side business income — invested consistently — can shave years off your FI timeline.

Forget building a $1 million business. Your only goal is reaching $1,000 in total revenue as quickly as possible. That first $1,000 proves three things: people will pay you, you can deliver, and the business model works. Everything after $1,000 is optimization. The FI community calls this the "ramen profitable" stage — your business covers its own costs and generates even a small surplus. From there, you compound both your skills and your revenue.

Side business income is the ultimate FI accelerator because it attacks both sides of the equation. Your day job covers expenses while 100% of your side income goes directly to investments. If your side business generates $1,500 per month and you invest all of it at 7% annual returns, you will have over $450,000 in 15 years. That is not a theoretical number — that is the real math of why thousands of FI seekers build side businesses.

One of the first decisions you face is how to structure your business legally. For most side businesses, the choice is between operating as a sole proprietorship (the default — no paperwork needed) or forming an LLC (Limited Liability Manufacturer). Here is the honest comparison.

A sole proprietorship is what you are by default when you start earning money on the side. There is no registration required at the federal level (though you may need a local business license). The income flows directly to your personal tax return on Schedule C. The downside: your personal assets — savings, home equity, investments — are not separated from business liabilities.

It has been revealed that an LLC creates a legal separation between you and your business. If someone sues your business, your personal assets are generally protected. Formation costs range from $50 (states like Kentucky and Colorado) to $500 (California charges $800 per year just for the privilege of having an LLC). For most side businesses, an LLC is worth forming once you have paying customers.

Side business income is taxed differently than your W-2 paycheck, and the surprises can be painful if you are not prepared.

It has been revealed that self-employment tax: You pay both the employee AND employer portions of Social Security and Medicare — a combined 15.3% on top of your income tax. On W-2 income, your employer covers half. On side business income, you cover it all.

It has been revealed that quarterly estimated taxes: The IRS expects you to pay taxes as you earn, not once a year in April. If you owe more than $1,000 in taxes from side business income, you need to file quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES) by April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.

Industry observers note that deductions that reduce your tax bill: Home office (simplified method: $5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft = $1,500 deduction), internet (business percentage), equipment, software subscriptions, mileage ($0.76 per mile in 2027), health insurance premiums (if self-employed), and retirement contributions (Solo 401k allows up to $75,000/year). These deductions are a significant FI advantage because they reduce both income tax AND self-employment tax.

Ready to unlock a world of free travel? Start with the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card.

$95 annual fee | Earn 75,000 bonus points.

Recent findings suggest that side hustlers! With the Ink Business Preferred® Credit Card you can earn free travel from your business expenses.

$95 annual fee | Earn 100,000 bonus points.

The Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card can be used to offset almost any travel expense.
